speechtext: I again desire to ask the Government a question in Tegard to the high cost of living in the Yukon. I have been favoured with another telegram on the subject which I should like to bring to the attention of the Government. It is dated Dawson, Yukon Territory, June 29, and reads as follows:

speechtext: I assume that the hon. member purposes to lay the groundwork for a question?

speechtext:
I stated that I was going to ask a question in regard to the matter. The telegram reads:
Dawson, Y.T., June 29, 1917. Hon. Frank Oliver,
Ottawa, Ont.
Ottawa despatches state Dawson business men deny our statements and claim allegations of administrator complying with dealers unfounded. We never alleged administrator was dealers' accomplice. We stated administrator evinced sympathy and partiality to companies and that local administration was obedient servant big business. We repeat statements. Given opportunity will prove them. Situation for working people is desperate ; growing worse daily: quick action necessary, hence these telegrams. We pay for ours; business men tell us Government frank theirs, and that they were asked to eulogize administrator in theirs but flatly refused. Eighty per cent local business people alien. Ninety per cent alien born. Few women in our leagues but have relatives at front. Our word is good as aliens. We demand proper investigation Pueblo mine disaster. Six men killed last March through inexcusable negligence. Prompt inspection demanded before new force one hundred men commence work as contemplated. We ask immediate investigation high cost of living; adjustment labour troubles between our companies and employees; suspension and investigation Administrator Williams; better service to Yukon from Dawson news in return for many thousands federal and territorial monies. Failing this our last appeal to Premier we appeal to Canadian public. Prompt and considerate action regarding telegram June first would have averted strike. Our Anal word, wages must go up or extortionate prices come down.
Geraldine Sharp,
Secretary Yukon Women's Protective League.
Marie Fotheringham,
Secretary Yukon Progressive League.
I wish to ask the Government if the strike alluded to here is still in progress, and also if the price of flour still remains as it was stated to be in the telegram I read to the House some weeks ago.

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING AND ON THE AMENDMENTS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in approaching the consideration of this very important question, I do so with

the desire and with the feeling that dt is the duty of every hon. member of this House to face the conditions as they exist in this country at the present time. I need not, and will not, refer to many of the addresses which have been made to this House, in which, I think, the real condition and position of Canada have, to a very large extent, been disregarded. I consider it is the duty of every member of this House, and of every citizen of this country, to be animated by two feelings at this time: First, that we may, to the best of our ability, render the best service, and play our full part as a nation in this war for freedom, and against the military despotism of Germany. Secondly, that we may have peace at home, present a united front to the enemy and keep our country free from discord and division, so that we will be worthy of the effort our sons are making, and evoke for Canada their pride and devotion when the boys come home again.
Mr. Speaker, for myself I have no misgivings as to the attitude that the individual Canadian should assume at this time. This is not an occasion when one should worry over the problem whether or not we are fighting for Britain. We are fighting, Sir, for Britain and with Britain. We are fighting for France and with France; for the United States of America, for Italy, for Russia; we are fighting for and with all those free countries, animated by a common purpose and idea, namely, that the militarism of Germany and the domination of that power which is attempted to be asserted by its ruler, may be put an end to, and that democracy and the rule of the people, may be the guiding element in the days that are to come. That cause is one which is so high, so noble, and so worthy that, let me say, Mr. Speaker, had the right hon. gentleman, who is the Premier of this country, appreciated that these were the real issues in this war, long ago all the forces of this country would have been mobilized, in order that we might render, in every way, to our cause, the best possible service. Long ago it was the duty of my right hon. friend to have conferred with Great Britain, with France, and, during the last two months, with the United States, as to what our part should be in this war, and what was the best service that we could render to this great cause. First, as to the food supply upon which these nations can rely, and which we can produce. There comes across the sea, from the old land-which those of us, Scotch, English and Irish,

are proud to call our home land-a call for food for the people. There comes also a further call, which my right hon. friend has not heeded in that he, by conference, should have arranged with the Allies as to the proper supply of our munitions, our minerals and our mineral products, which they require, and which they should have from us. He should have arranged to determine as to the transportation which we were to provide and to the ships in which we could transport the products of our Dominion to the Mother Country.
In addition to that, there should have been a conference as to the number of men that we should furnish, having regard to our population and to the needs at the front. In reference to all of these matters, there should have been conference and mobilization long ago. To the extent that my right hon. friend lagged in his duty and put off the making of proper arrangements in regard to all these matters, he has been responsible for failure and is to be blamed for the present condition under which Canada is not giving her full service to the Mother Country, If we had to-day what we should have had long ago, a proper mobilization and organization of all these resources, a geneious, united and enthusiastic people would, have seen that all things necessary were supplied. But, instead of deliberate organization and mobilization of our resources, what have we had since the war began? Nothing but hysteria. Month after month, year after year, instead of calm deliberation and cool attention to those conditions which history tells us are necessary to victory, we have been going from one hysteria to the other, without regard to consequences. For instance, at the beginning of the war the Government, instead of providing machine guns and making them available for war purposes, permitted the raising of subscriptions throughout the country for this and other purposes, without the slightest guidance or direction. A generous response was made by the people to whom these appeals were directed in no organized form. But since the handing over of the money to the Government, what evidence have we of any organization in regard to matters of that kind?
Every hon. gentleman in this House has been waiting for the election contest which my right hon. friend kept hanging over the heads of the people.

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING AND ON THE AMENDMENTS.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING AND ON THE AMENDMENTS.
speechtext:
On no less than three occasions indisputable evidences were given of my right hon. friend's intention to precipitate an election. In 1915 the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Robert Rogers) stated in this House that in respect of such a petty question in war time as representation in the Senate the people of Canada were calling upon the Government in tones of thunder to bring on an election. My right hon. friend yielded to the efforts of that gentleman to this extent: ballots were printed, ballot boxes were sent to England, and every preparation was made for an election. Since then the same condition has gone on. My right hon. friend has been keen in his regard for political considerations; and now, in the light of a condition arising for the first time and affecting the whole country, he suggests that politics should be forgotten for the moment and that we should face this condition together.
Then, take the story of the national service propaganda last year. By virtue of the last powers given him by the War Measures Act, my right hon. friend appointed a commission which he called the National Service Commission. He quarrelled with the chairman of that commission over a question of political patronage, and then appointed the member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) as chairman. Then a campaign was carried on throughout the country-for what? Was there no wastage at the front last year? Was it not necessary last year that the places of the boys who went out and died should be filled? Did my hon. friend find out only a month ago that there was wastage at the front? My right hon. friend and his colleague went through the country discussing matters of patriotic concern. But it turns out now, after the propaganda is all over, that the object of that campaign was not to secure the filling of wastages at the front, but to find men to work on the farms and in other places.
Then, take the absolutely undignified incident that occurred only six months ago, the dispute that arose between the right hon. gentleman and the then Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes). The letters which were made public at that time had no parallel in English or Canadian parliamentary history. If the statements they contained were true, those letters disclosed a condition of affairs within the cabinet which showed that the Government were not worrying about filling the wastages at the front. These are a few of the curious performances which have characterized
the administration of hon. gentlemen opposite in connection with the war.
The hysteria seems to have affected some hon. gentlemen on this side. Take, for instance, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark). Last year the member for Red Deer gave evidence of being affected by hysteria. When criticisms of a most legitimate and proper character were being made by gentlemen on this side with a view to seeing that the administration of military affairs in Canada should be wisely carried on, that hon. gentleman undertook to denounce every one of his former confreres. A similar obsession seemed to have affected the hon. gentleman some few weeks ago.

When hon. gentlemen recall that the member for Red Deer was one of those in Great Britain who preached against Great Britain's taking any part in securing the freedom of South Africa they will wonder whether there is not something in the suggestion'of hysteria. I would remind hon. gentlemen, also, that a little over a year ago the member for Red Deer intimated that he was proud of the position taken by Sir John Simon, who retired from the British Government because he did not believe in conscription, and that he had congratulated Sir John Simon upon his sturdy defence of Liberalism. I have some ground, therefore, for suggesting that the member for Red Deer has been affected by some sort of hysteria. Fortunately, the plain people of this land, who have been watching what the Government has been doing, have not been afflicted with hysteria. Where the people have had opportunity of expressing their views in respect of provincial affairs their votes have been against the Conservative party, largely, if not wholly, on account of the way the Government has been managing Canada's part in the war. Let me give you an illustration. A little over a week ago there was an election in Saskatchewan. The slogan of the Conservative party in that election campaign was: vote for Willoughby, the Conservative leader, and for Borden. That campaign cry was met in this way by the Regina Leader:-
It means expressing approval of the Borden Government's military administration, Including its "political colonels." the profiteering in mu-

the Interior Department to the effect that conscription was not deemed either advisable or necessary in Canada, I would like to ask the Minister of Militia and Defence whether it is the intention of the Government to change their policy in regard to enlistment and provide for a policy of conscription, or whether they intend to put in force compulsorily the provisions, of the Militia Act.
During all that time the men were dying at the front just as they are now; the losses were just as great if not greater. What do you think, Sir, the then Minister of Militia replied in answer to my question,? He said:

speechtext:
Then the right hon. gentleman had not taken the opportunity to consult about it. Let me show him what would have taken place under this proposition. Were the election held in October it would not be possible for the newly organized Parliament to be in existence here until November. After November, according to this Bill, local boards would have to be appointed all over this country. After the local boards were appointed every man who claimed exemption from service could makfe his appeal to the county court, afterwards to the judge of the Superior Court in his district, and afterwards even to the Supreme Court of Canada. Men could not be mobilized for training until the spring of 1918. And, if my right hon. friend will ask his Minister of Militia with regard to the time necessary to train men and transport them across the ocean, he will learn that they could not have had a man in France until the autumn of 1918, as I have said.
Now, there are in this House five groups in relation to this measure. First, there are those who are in favour of the six months' hoist of this Bill, who practically say that Canada has done enough in the war and are opposed to conscription in any form or at any time. Second, there are those who are anxious that Canada should play the full part of which she is capable in this war, and who desire, in order that disunion should be avoided, that the principle of the Bill should be submitted to the people for ratification before it goes into force. Third, there are those who favour the Bill, but are
anxious that further efforts should be made for voluntary recruiting before the Bill is proclaimed. Fourth, there are those who want to pass the Bill as it stands, but not to enforce it until after an election. And, fifth, there are those who want the Bill passed and put into force immediately. For the benefit of the gentlemen who take any one of the last four grounds, I should like to discuss the Bill in principle for a moment or two.
I take the ground that this Bill is not a bona fide attempt to deal with the problem, and I propose to prove that from the evidence contained in the Bill itself. In the first place, there is no provision for the registration of the man-power of this nation. In Great Britain, where conscription was ultimately adopted, there were, first, various schemes of registratkm-the Lord Derby scheme and others. All the preliminaries were gone through by which the authorities learned the number of men in Great Britain, with particulars about every man-his age, occupation, capacities, all the needed information-so that when the time came to send out the recruiting officer that recruiting officer could put his hand on the man he wanted. In the United States they dealt with this problem sternly, properly, as it would have been dealt with in Canada if this Government had not been absolutely ineffective from the beginning. In the United States a simple method was provided under which the aid of the municipal authorities all over that great republic was enlisted to make a roll of the available men. On the tenth day of June, when the labours of the day were concluded, there were forwarded to the military authorities of the United States complete statements of the man-power of the nation, showing, with relation to every man, bis age, residence, trade, or occupation, and all other necessary facts. When they require these men they know where to find them. Have we in Canada had any registration, any attempt to bring home to the people the sternness of the situation, any attempt to put down in black and white the facts with regafd to our manpower, so that the authorities may know what that man-power is?
Have we anything of that kind in this Bill? No, there is nothing of the kind. When the Bill was introduced, I asked the right hon. gentleman whether he intended to have registration, and he said he did not. I say that the absence of a provision for registration is evidence that the Government do not intend to put this Bill into effect with any degree of haste. Having

failed to provide for registration, what are they going on for their data? They are going on the census which is seven years old, and they are going on the National Service data. The National Service data was obtained, according to the statement made by responsible labour men in this country, under the representation that National Service was not for men to fight but for men to work. Do you not think that that is a very singular and very peculiar kind of basis for people to start from who are anxious to deal with this problem in a stern way in keeping with all the eloquent addresses we have heard in this House? The evidence of the failure to grapple with this question from the standpoint of the gentlemen who hold views such as I have mentioned, is beyond all doubt. Take, for instance, the men in the first class from twenty years up: How is the gentleman who has to deal with this matter from a military standpoint to ^find out from the census returns or from any other source the whereabouts of a boy who was eighteen years old two years ago, when this war began? How are you ever going to get the names? Where is the gentleman who is going to mobilize these people to get the data on which to start? It is absolutely impossible under this Bill. Why, Sir, in the United States they provide that every man between eighteen and forty-five having no dependents of any kind and not engaged in employment essential to the national security had to register on a certain day; they had all the names of these people on the register. My hon. friends are not proceeding in that way.
Take the provision in regard to the Board of Selection. My right hon. friend (Sir Robert Borden) claimed great credit for the method of appointing local tribunals. That is subsection 3 of section 6 which reads as follows:
Each local tribunal shall consist of two members. One member shall be appointed by a Board of Selection to be established by joint resolution of the Senate and House of Commons.
That means, when you get it translated into ordinary Anglo-Saxon, that the Government of Canada, through their appointees on that Board of Selection, are going to appoint one of the members of the local board, and the consequence will be that you have the same pernicious political influence that has blasted the ideals of a large number of the Canadian people, in operation under this Bill. If a county court judge is a good enough man to select one member of this local board, he is good

enough to select two. There can be no possible justification, unless there is a desire to interject politics into this question, for this Government reserving to itself the appointment of one of the members of these local boards, through the committee of selection. If the Bill proposed is bona fide, let a county court judge appoint both. If he is a person to appoint one member of the boiard, he is a proper person to appoint the other.
Why all this elaboration in regard to appeals, if the need is so great and my right hon. friend is sincere? You will have this result:	The man who has money
enough to go and retain a lawyer to raise' the legal question as to the meaning of "national interest" in the first three exemption clauses can carry his case to the Supreme Court of Canada, while the poor beggar at home who has not enough money to fee a lawyer cannot appeal. The man with money can prolong his hearing for months and months. The evidence is that these gentlemen do not believe in their hearts that there is such urgent necessity, because if they did so believe they would have a Bill of such a character that there would be no question about it.
Then, let us come to the proposition as to what national interest is. I asked my right hon. friend when he introduced this Bill whether there would be any definition by this House of the words "national interest." My right hon. friend said there would he none, that it was proposed to define national interest by the regulations that were to be made by the Government. In other words, this Government is reserving to itself the right to say who shall go and who shall not go. Respecting to the full, as I do, the position taken by men in this country who believe that conscription is imperative at this moment, I say that when this Government reserves to itself the right to define national interest, it thereby wipes out all the enthusiasm of these people, and when the people come to study this thing closely, they will realize that this Government is playing politics more than anything else.
Are the agriculturists of this country to be exempted or are they not? My hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) frankly told the people of Quebec the other day that they need not worry about this Bill; they were nearly all farmers, and they were going to be exempt. Is there anything of that kind in the Bill? Nothing of xhs kind. The words "national interest" are left entirely in the hands of this

Government, to give whatever definition of it they like.
Let us look at the figures as to the occupations of the different people in Canada as defined by the census of 1911. I am giving now the figures of all those from ten years of age to the oldest man in the country. The numbers engaged in the different occupations were as follows: Agriculture, 917,848; building trades, 245,990; domestic and personal service, 75,133; civil and municipal government, 72,531; fishing and hunting, 42,901; manufacturing, 392,781; mining, 62,706; professions, 62,781; trade and merchandise, 240,903; transportation (which includes sailors and railway men and so on), 210,692, making a total of 2,358,813. Now, is this Bill intended to exempt agriculturists ? I should like to know from the right hon. gentleman. I pause for a reply.

My hon. friend is capable of reading the Bill and drawing his own conclusions. As to the particular provisions, this is not the time to discuss them. We shall discuss them in committee.
Mr. MACDONALDWith all deference to my right hon. friend, I think this is the time, and I think it is about time that somebody in this discussion did find out what this Bill is providing for.
I want to know, and the country wants to know, whether the 917,848 men who are engaged in agriculture are to be exempted, or whether they are not. I want to know what the Solicitor General, who did discuss the details of the Bill, meant when he intimated to the people of Quebec that they need not worry about this thing. He said they had large families, that they got married young, that they were all working on the farms, and they need not worry about it. The Prime Minister will not tell me whether that is so or not. There is in the preamble of the Bill this statement:
And Whereas, by reason of the large number of men who have already left agricultural and industrial pursuits In Canada to join such Expeditionary Force as volunteers, and of the necessity of sustaining, under such conditions, the productivity of the Dominion, it is expedient to secure the men still required, not by ballot as provided in the Militia Act, but by selective draft.
That is in the preamble, but not in the enacting clauses. All that is in the enacting clause of the Bill is the proviso that the man who can show a local board that it is in the national interest that he should continue in the employment he is then engaged in, may be exempt. The Solicitor General indicated that the farmers were to be exempt. Connected with industries, manufacturing and industrial plants we have 392,000 men. In other words, in the agricultural and industrial classes there are 1,300,000, so that 200,000 more than half the working people of Canada are connected with those two industries. In Great Britain, they do not take the sailors or the rail-waymen. In Canada there are 210,000 transportation employees. Adding these figures, we have 1,500,000 men exempted. Then what about the miners, Mr. Speaker? Are the miners to be taken, or are they not? They are an essential element in this country. We are appointing commissions giving complete control to gentlemen to deal with this problem of the production of coal, in order that next winter our people may not freeze to death. Are the miners of Canada to be taken under this Bill? Then there are 34,547 men engaged in the fishing industry in Canada. In Great Britain they are exempt. In Canada they are the greatest producers of cheap food that you can find all over the country. If these gentlemen on the other side of the House had organized the national resources of this country, the cost of living in central Canada would not have been so great as it is. If the fish obtained in the Maritime Provinces and on the Pacific coast had been taken to our Canadian cities, it would have reduced the cost of living. Should the fishermen be conscripted? In the United States, I observe they exempt civil and municipal government employees, which classes make 72,531 in Canada. Are they to he exempt in Canada? There are men in the professions, 62,781. There is no question about them. I guess they will have to go. No doubt the lawyers and the doctors will have to go.

Referring to the
lumbering industry of Canada, the number of men engaged in forestry is 42,901. Are those men to go? I am citing these figures for the purpose of showing that it is about time, in the discussion of this serious measure, that we had some pronouncement to the country as to what is really meant by this Bill.	Are we
going to leave it in the hands of this Government to say what national



interest means, and to s;y that Tom Jones has to go and Dick Smith may stay? Any one familiar with the conditions in England and Scotland knows that, as a result of having left to the local boards in Great Britain the sole determination of this question of national interest, the gravest dissatisfaction has arisen. There is a suspicion of favouritism. There is a feeling that there has been discrimination, and in the operation and carrying out of the measure, conditions of the gravest character which should not have arisen now prevail, and the consequence is that the poorer people of the Old Country are discontented. My right hon. friend must have heard that when he was over there. My right hon. friend has another proposition-

speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman tell me what he is going to suggest on this point, when the House goes into committee?

I will give my right hon. friend many suggestions. I will give him one at once. My hon. friend has, as I say, for political purposes merely, introduced a measure, the details of which he declines to explain, and, in the interests of the country, I am calling the attention of the people to the fact that the Prime Minister will not furnish an explanation. I will give the hon. gentleman an illustration. Paragraph "C" of section 11, referring to exemptions, reads:
That it is expedient in the national interest that, instead of being employed in the military service, he should continue to be educated or trained for any work for which he is then being educated or trained.	.
What does that mean? It means that if one has a boy between 20 and 25 years of age going to college, and can afford to keep him there, and can afford to go to the local board and say, "Here is a boy I am educating and training, and it is important he should finish his education and training," that boy can stay at home, while the son of the poor man, who does not go to college, who has to work for his living, and get it as best he can, has not the advantage of that exemption. I say that exemption should be wiped out.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

Subsection "D" ,of section 11 reads:
That serious hardship would ensue if the man were placed on active service, owing to his exceptional financial or business obligations or domestic position.
Let me give an instance. Dealing with the case of the poor man dependent upon

his daily work for a living, who has purchased a home on the instalment plan, or having gotten his home together, has obtained some furniture on the instalment plan and not paid for it, does he come within this category? I think not. I think this means that a man between the age of 20 and 45, who is engaged in some important business, can pay a lawyer, go before the Board and prove that his financial position is such, and the matters depending upon him are such, that he should be exempt. In the eyes of the man who wants to perform full service in this great cause, is there any reason why the poor man should be taken, and the rich man left at home? That will happen under that section.

speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman favour striking out that provision?

speechtext:
I certainly would not permit a clause of that kind to be put in without a definition, so that there would be no discrimination against the poor man, as there apparently is, in that section, as drawn. Why, in this curious measure, should a clause be inserted that it should not come into effect except by Order in Council? There is no more reason why this Bill should not go into effect on the day that His Excellency gives assent to it than there is why any Bill passed by Parliament should not become effective when sanctioned. My hon. friend may have some good reason for inserting that provision. He may have an election in mind, but I warn the Prime Minister that many a man whose soul is stirred will be keeping his eye on him when he decides to make this provision.
This Bill is based on a peculiar statement in the preamble. You will observe that in the preamble, after reciting the provisions of the Militia Act, the clause says:
And whereas enough men do not volunteer to provide such reinforcements.
In other words, according to all geneses upon which legislation is perfected, if men volunteer in sufficient numbers, there is no need for this Bill. I decline to assent to the suggestion that voluntary enlistment in Canada has failed. If it has lagged behind; if the youth of the Land have not responded as they should, it is the fault of the Government. In the first place, more inducements of a material character should have been held out to the men who were asked to go to the front. To ask a man who had a family depending upon him to give up his work and accept 51.10

a day as a private was not calculated to lead men. to believe that the state was generous in its dealings with volunteers. More 'harm has been done to recruiting by the manner in which the assigned pay and separation allowances have been handled than has been done in any other way. Many wives who were depending upon their 55 cents a day did not get their cheque when the (month oamie( laround; others did not get their separation allowances when they should have got them. Would that have a tendency to arouse enthusiasm iamong the people? Wives of men at the front have begged members of the House to intercede for them at Ottawa and endeavour to have their money sent to them. These persons have spoken to their friends .and relatives about the way they were being treated. Would that instil enthusiasm into the people? Why did not the Government insure the lives of men who left dependents behind them, in order that, without legal technicalities or red tape, their relatives would be enabled to get a certain sum of money if injury should come to their dear ones who had gone away?
Then, Sir, -consider the breaking up of the regiments. Consider the extent to which sentimental ties were broken when regiments were disbanded. Look at the way the Irish boys of Montreal were treated. Consider the conditions in my own province. By vigorous effort, there were organized four battalions which were full of the sentiment and enthusiasm that are characteristic of men of the -Scottish race. These battalions went o-ut with the full assurance that they would go to the front as units. A week after they landed on the other side, 'an order came for a draft. They -used to tell us that the British -authorities asked for these drafts, -but the British authorities did not ask for this draft; it was asked for and made by the Canadian authorities in Great Britain appointed by this Government. When they made the draft, did they take one of the battalions and send it over with its officers? No; they proceeded to slash the whole of the four battalions, crippling and destroying them, so that to-day only two remain out of the four that left our province to fight together in this great cause. Is that calculated to arouse the enthusiasm of the boys whom we have been asking to volunteer? Not at all.

speechtext:
I am -showing that
th-is Government says: As a result of our
188J
maladministration, mistakes and failures, we cannot get any more recruits; therefore, we -must have conscription.
I need not relate the -story of political management in connection with the war; it is known everywhere. The purchase of supplies was placed in the hands of local patronage committees ; no medical men who were not Conservatives were permitted to examine recruits and the ideals of our people were blunted.
Let -me say here that the country has a right to know definitely the circumstances in connection with the stopping of recruiting a year ago. On the one hand we have a positive and definite statement made in this House by the exMinister of Militia, and on the other hand we have a modified denial by the Prime Minister. The country has a right to know what occurred between these two gentlemen, and whether or not recruiting was halted, if not stopped, as a result of anything that took place last year. If the efforts in the matter of recruiting had been maintained with all the vigour and enthusiasm of previous years, there would have been no necessity for throwing this apple of discord, the Military Service Bill, before the Canadian people.
The people of Canada have no faith in the present militia officials of this Government. We had in this country various generals whose names were household words when they were sent over here by the British Government. They were such men- of recognized ability in military matters a6 Lord Dundonald, General Lake, General Mackenzie. How many people in Canada ever heard of the man who is now general officer commanding the forces in this country? Who ever saw him commanding any of the military camps in Canada? What influence has his personality upon the Canadian people? Who ever heard tell of General Cwatkin- except a few persons in Ottawa? Australia has its General Birdwood, whose name is a household word in that Dominion, and who takes overseas the men who enlist under him. Who is this General Gwatkin-, upon whom the Canadian, people 'are asked to pin their faith as their military leader? The present Minister of Militia and his parliamentary secretary are genial men, but what do they know of military organization? What have they tried to leara? They have simply marked time. If you want to find out anything about anybody on the other side, you are told: We will cable to England and find out. If a soldier is seriously wounded, many weary

days must /pass before information can be gained as to what has happened to him. The methods of the Goviemment in this respect have caused the people to feel that the present Administration is weak, inefficient and incompetent.
I am rather inclined to inquire of some of the gentlemen opposite who have been overseas as to what is the actual position occupied by Sir George Perley, whose title is Overseas Minister of Militia. If they would speak frankly I know what they would say. I have here a letter that was written by a colonel in England on the last day of March:
There never was such dissatisfaction in the world as exists in the Canadian forces, ail things seem to be subordinated to politics, and pull, and everybody here recognizes it. I have heard many men who have been prominent Conservatives all their lives; some have been members at Ottawa, and others of provincial Houses, declare that all they wanted was a chance to get even with the present Government.
Indeed, it is stated that a certain member of the other side of this House has said that when he took his battalion overseas, he took over 1,100 Conservatives, and when he returned he left 1,100 opponents ,of this Government behind him. This colonel makes this further statement:
The present Canadian administration in London are trying to gain the confidence of the forces, and I think General Turner is honest in his work. I had a talk with him the other day and he assured me there was no politics in the present appointments, but when you notice Bob Roger's son as his personal aide sitting outside his door, and Major Montague, a son of the doctor of that name, in the next room, and when you have to see these men and state your business before you cap see the General, even if you have a definite appointment, then you begin to wonder what the game is, and it is the same all through everything, if you have not a political standing, you don't count.
I take from the Calgary News-Telegram a letter written on June 22, by Private A. H. McPherson, No. 116838, 11th O.B., C.M.E.:
It is the duty of every young man who has no one to support but himself to enlist and help out his country in time of trouble. In this way there would be no need for conscription. I do not think it a good policy for a "rump" government to pass conscription without first putting it to the people. In this way our country will be saved and brought into unity. Otherwise, I fear there is going to be a rupture, and I am of the opinion that the Prime Minister was right when he said that he dreaded the coming home of the boys from the trenches. There was some truth in his statement that he dreaded their coming.
When such statements are made with reference to the voluntary system of re-

cruiting and everything else in connection with the management of the war and the leadership of the men who have gone forth so gladly and proudly to fight; is it any wonder that we ask here that there should be some regeneration, a development of new ideals in this House and in this country? That is the situation.
I said in the beginning that I would speak of conditions and not of theories. I have attempted to outline briefly and as earnestly and effectively as I know how the facts as they appear to me and they cannot be questioned.
Some very unkind statements have been made as to the attitude of the labouring classes. I have seen in the Conservative newspapers published in my province a very abusive article reflecting upon Mr. J. C. Watters. I have known Mr. Watters for the last four or five years, and any one who has met him must agree with me that he is a very thoughtful gentleman, and, in my opinion, one of the highest type of men who have ever been connected with labour in this country. He has had the confidence of- this Government. My right hon. friend and his Government appointed Mr. J. C. Watters on that Economic Commission which was created by the Government. When there was a conference at Washington a short time ago with the representatives Of Great Britain who came over here, Mr. J. C. Watters was one of the men whom this Government selected to take down to Washington with their representatives to confer upon questions relating to the war. Therefore when Mr. Watters speaks on these matters, we have no right to disregard him. We can not say that, because the sons of labour have gone out and fought valiantly in this war, their brethren at home have no right to express their views. The labour leaders represent 160,000 men associated with labour in this country, and in dealing with an important -question of this character, we should carefully consider their position. You cannot brush them aside and tell them that -they are slackers, or traitors. TKey represent a large body of people, and Mr. Watters is a gentleman of the highest possible ideals. The labour people say that they went to the Prime Minister and discussed these questions from time to time. They say: When our organization at Vancouver took a position in regard to this question of conscription, and when later on, at Toronto, we dealt with this matter, we proposed the nationalization of all the aids necessary and the conscription of all the power of the nation for

the prosecution of the war. We cannot find fault with them for that. We may not all of us agree with them as to the nationalization of all t)he industries of this country, but when these gentlemen, at this time, when the future of Canada is at stake, submit these matters to us for our consideration and say to us: We must have conscription of all the resources of the nation, you can- not 'brush these people aside;
5 p.m. they must be heard, and if their plea is a good one it must he considered. In the proceedings of the Trades and Labour Congress, held last year, they stated their position in regard to munitions as follows:-
When it was known by the Executive Council that the conditions resulting from the outbreak of war would necessitate the manufacture of munitions in Canada, it was urged that the Government undertake the same by utilizing their various shops for that purpose. . . .
All things being equal as between Government shops and those of a contractor, the same conditions as to hours of labour and as to quantity and quality of work performed, the Government, by undertaking its own work, saves the profits otherwise taken by the contractor, the amount of which profits can be distributed in the shape of higher wages to the employee and at reduced cost to the Government. This has been demonstrated in Great Britain, South Africa, New Zealand and Australia.
They ask that such action should he taken. They say: Hand in hand with conscription of men, if you are going to have that, let us have conscription in other things also. Have they not a right to he heard? In the circular issued last year by Mr. Watters, after the National Service propaganda had begun, and when certain of his associates had complained because he had asked them to sign these cards and return them, he made this statement:-
At the three conventions of the Congress held since the outbreak of war the policy adopted was to "lend every assistance possible to the Allies in a mighty endeavour to secure early and final victory for the cause of freedom and democracy." This policy was qualified at the Vancouver convention by the adoption of "unchangeable opposition to all that savours of conscription." At the Toronto convention the war policy of the Congress was still further modified by opposing registration. . . .
The opposition to registration which developed at the Toronto convention was based on the assumption that it was only a preliminary step to conscription such as had taken place in Great Britain. There is a wide difference, however, between the system adopted in Great Britain and that in Canada. The purposes of the two systems are, also, very dissimilar, according to the statement made by the Premier, Sir Robert L. Borden.
The system of registration put into operation in Great Britain led to conscription, the Bystem of registration in Canada is designed to lead away from conscription. The Prime Minister and the Director General of the National Service Board were both emphatic in their assertions as to there being no connection between registration and conscription. They were equally emphatic as to the purely voluntary nature of the service to be rendered for military, industrial and agricultural purposes in calling on every individual to fill out the cards. The purpose, as vouched for by the First Minister of the Dominion, of the registration plan, therefore, is to secure such information as will demonstrate how and in what particular our efforts may be best directed to give effect to the declared war policy of the Congress itself.
Should the Government undertake to adopt military or even industrial conscription a wholly different state of affairs would obtain. The action of the Vancouver convention, reaffirmed at Toronto, clearly sets forth the position of the Congress in unqualified opposition to conscription.
That was penned last summer before the question of conscription was raised, and it was given as a defence by Mr. Watters to critics, because he had asked the labour men to sign and return the cards because he had the assurance of the Prime Minister that the cards meant, not conscription, but merely registration .
Here is another statement:
If the Government is sincere in its determination to "consecrate the power of the nation" to the cause of the Allies and democracy and not dictated to nor influenced by "Downing Street," or the dominating privileged interests in Canada nor simply actuated by miserable political party considerations, the conscription of man power will follow and not precede that of wealth and the nationalization of every industry necessary for the prosecution of the war. Until the Government gives proof that conscription is, in the words of the Prime Minister, "the only effective method to preserve the existence of the State and of the institutions and liberties which we enjoy," organized labor has every warrant in seeking its defeat by both their economic and political power.
That is the position of labour. They say to the people of Canada: If you are going to take men-and you told ns you were not -deal first with wealth and with the industries of this country, so that the best possible service can be given by the whole country to the war. They ask that the measure be submitted to the people for consideration, but that request is disregarded.
Now I come to the other problem that faces us, dealing' here with conditions again-and not with theories. We have in this country over 2,000,000 people who speak the French language. The census returns of seven years ago show that one out of every three men in this country speaks the French language. The position, therefore, of the province of Quebec in this Confederation cannot be ignored. We all know that the issue in the province of Quebec

we said we would not 'follow. We must not allow that for the sake of the Canada that is yet to be. We .must not create race divisions in this country. When I hear our friends talk about "these Frenchmen," I recall the history of the great nation to which we are so proud to belong. Are all the British race men of Saxon blood? No, Sir. They came to the tight little island people from many different nations of Europe-Angles, Saxons, Danes and Normans, and the Celts came to Scotland and Ireland.	In the old land they had
their difficulties of race, they had their problems to deal with, as we have in Canada. They worked out their destiny by good will and toleration, and they welded into one all these conflicting elements, making the imperial nation of today. Wie will follow where Britain has led, and by a policy of conciliation and good will among all the people of different nationalities, we will establish on this northern half of this continent a nation anxious only for the greatness of Canada, proud first and last of being Canadians and of being a nation within the great British Empire. Were that great leader, the late Sir John Macdonald, here to-day, animated by the feelings which guided him in dealing with these problems fifty years ago, he would tell how this situation should be met.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday, at a few minutes to eleven o'clock, I rose in this House to take up the discussion of this conscription Bill which we have been considering for more than two weeks. I had scarcely opened my mouth and uttered two words: "Mr. Speaker" when my hon. friend from Kimouski (Mr. Boulay) immediately sprang to his feet, upon a point of order, and asked if there was a quorum of the House. You had the roll called by the deputy Clerk of the House who stated, after taking down the names of the members present, that there was no quorum, so that the House was then adjourned until Tuesday, yestefiday, at three o'clock in the afternoon.
I may add, Mr. Speaker, that to-day, I will tell you immediately that I am against [DOT]conscription, in case my hon. friend for Rimouski should again rise on a point of order and there would1 be no quorum in this House. Therefore, I immediately declare myself against conscription.
This Bill, which we have been here discussing for over two weeks, is so far-reaching in its effects as regards the people of this country, that everyone is wondering where the Prime Minister is leading us to, as the Prime Minister has so often declared, in this House and elsewhere, that the pursuit of this war would forever be continued under the volunteering system.
In the .course of the debate, in this House, on January 17, 1916, the hon. Prime Minister, speaking after the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) declared, explicitly that there never would

be any conscription in this country. There is, therefore, nothing strange in the fact that the people of this country should want this war carried on without having such a measure of compulsion passed by Parliament.	i
As for me, I do not need this conscription Bill to say that I condemn the Government. On several occasions, I have spoken in this House about the carrying on of this war, stating that the Government had led us to bankruptcy, and after putting us in bankruptcy, they now want furthermore the blood of our children.
I agree with the great French and English statesmen. I have always agreed with the big London dailies which have, almost all of them, declared in their columns that to ask the people of Canada 150,000 men, was an extraordinary effort, and that England would never ask so much.
The people of this country have decided to do more than that-T commend the soldiers who have volunteered and enlisted- but, unfortunately, those who will have to foot the bill, after the war, will think as I do, that the enlisting went too far, even voluntarily.
Conscription, in my hum'ble opinion, dates from the moment this Government has attempted to follow in the footsteps of the British government. We have had, some six months ago, the National Service cards, the Government wanting to know the man power of the nation, so they said. Our good papers of Montreal and all over the country, among them that sanctimonious Patrie of Montreal, which circulates in our counties declare day after day in its columns that there was no harm in signing those National Service cards; that the people should obey the State, and it was merely to know the man power of the nation, to work on the farms, to work in the ammunition factories, etc.
I had already declared, previously, in the county of Laprairie-Napierville, that this Government would surely bring about conscription, because I always remembered the statement made by the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) in his own province of Manitoba, that for this war, as he put it, we should give our last dollar and send our last man.
The hon. Solicitor General counts for much in this Government. It is he who gets the Government out of its difficulties, and I believe he is the Prime Minister's right bower. I may add, Mr. Speaker, that he is often called upon to defind its wrongdoings, for his party gets often enopgh in a quandary.
I therefore did tell them, at home, that we would have conscription. The Prime Minister has not fooled me; I know the Prime Minister better than my electors do, and even better than our bishops of the province of Quebec, who had taken his word and told us: submit, because the State demands it.
As to the National Service, my parish priest read that letter, which had been sent to him by his bishop and, after Divine service, I openly declared that I knew too well the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) too well to have faith in his word and I further stated that these National Service cards were a step towards conscription. I also declared that, in the cases of dogma and religion, I followed the bishop's advice, but that, in politics, I claimed to be better informed than he could possibly be. To-day, these same people admit that I had then spoken the truth and that, indeed, I knew what was going on.
The Government and the politicians, oT both parties, are not agreed upon this Military Service Act. Not being a lawyer, but a farmer, I will refrain from discussing pro or con, but I am comforted when I think that, in a general way, laws are made so that nobody can understand them.

speechtext:
The reason is to enable lawyers to make use of their accomplishments, and I am not at all surprised when I see that they do not quite agree upon this Compulsory Service Act. But, Mr. Speaker, this legal entanglement has, nevertheless, a bad side; it makes our judges grow old too soon and, consequently, we have to pay them pensions too young. At -all events, I am glad that we have an ex-jtidge as Minister of Justice; he grasps my meaning and he may perhaps extend his cooperation towards changing present conditions. Now, that he enjoys fairly good health, that he has recovered his nerve and [DOT]-no mean consideration,-that he receives a fair indemnity as a retired judge, minister and deputy, I say that he should turn all his efforts to improving the Militia Act of this country or any other Act, so that we may be able to discuss them in an intelligent way. Why not insert in the Militia Act that our troops shall be levied only for the defence of Canada, unconditionally? Now, Mr. Speaker, the best evidence of the fact that the Government do not undei'-stand our laws, as I stated a moment ago, is that they have not seen fit to rely upon the existing Militia Act, to levy volunteers

and send them overseas. After all, that Militia Act may perhaps not toe as bad as might be imagined, since the Government could not use it for sending our troops away.
Upon several occasions, I have declared, in this House, that I was in favour of a reasonable participation in this war; even to-day, I am of the same mind, and 1 believe all rational people will suport me in such an attitude; but when the people of this country are asked to bleed themselves to such an extent, I say: Let us stop, it is more than time to do it.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what are the reasons given by the Prime Minister to justify the introduction of this conscription Bill? The reasons alleged are that our soldiers are loudly demanding reinforcements and, secondly, that we have trenches to defend in France and in Flanders. To this, I reply that we have no trenches in France, not having been consulted before the declaration of war and that, probably, we will not be consulted either when the matter of signing peace comes up. To my mind, it AVas Canada's duty to aid the Allies in this war, but, I repeat it, having had nothing to do with the declaration of war, I maintain that we have no trenches to defend in Europe and that the countries who have and who must defend their trenches are France, England and .Italy, but not Canada. That is why I oppose, as forcibly as I can, the sending of men to the other side.
We must be fair, Mr. Speaker. The son must assist his father, but he must do so according to his means. If, in helping his father, the son is going to ruin, I say that it is his duty to refuse his assistance. Applying that simile to Canada-and it is appropriate-I say that we must not go any further. I have spoken of this ticklish war question with many people and every one of them has told me that the stand I have taken in this House is surely that which should be taken by all the members and by the Prime Minister himself, if they have at heart the interests of the people whom they represent, before siding with the nations of Europe.

speechtext:
(Translation) Even the leader of the Opposition?
/Mr. LANCTOT: (Translation) Certainly. \A7hat did really happen during this journey to England of the Premier and of his two colleagues, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) and the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. R. Rogers)?
I presume that the Minister of Public Works has had a great deal to do with this

Bill for, if I can judge from what I read in the newspapers of this country, and especially in the papers friendly to the Minister of Public Works, something was needed to divert public poinion from the Minister of Public Works himself.
Mr. Speaker, you know that there has been a judgment rendered by a commission sitting in Winnipeg, out of which the Minister of Public Works has emerged something to the worse and on his last leg. Therefore, so as to face the electorate, it became somewhat necessary to save 'appearances, and, in order to shield a little the Minister of Public Works, to introduce this conscription Bill, so that nothing else could be discussed during the coming electoral campaign -Conscription will, in fact, be the main topic of discussion in Quebec and in Ontario; but it will he discussed from one point of view in Quebec and from another one in Ontario.
I believe that the Bill is the master stroke of the Minister of Public Works.
Mr. Speaker, this Bill, and the clauses of which I have read, is called a "Selective" bill. The Government will be able to take soldiers wherever they please. The friends of the Government will say in the West: This is not for you; in Ontario, again it will probably not toe for 'them, because they have done their duty, but we wish to reach Quebec, which has not given enough recruits,
The minister who just now represents the province of Quebec, Hon. Mr. Sevigny, was in Quebec last Sunday; he has given every one his share in Quebec; toe is going to send from the city of Montreal 10,000 men; from the city of Quebec 1,000; from the 'municipalities, which number 1,200, ten each, I believe. That is not much, so he says, but I would like to know who are those who are ready to go, from Montreal, from Quebec and all the municipalities?
As the hon. minister belongs to the old city of Champlain, to Quebec city; as he is strongly in favour of conscription and of war, I do hope he will be the first one to leave Quebec and give the example to the other young men of that city to go and fight the good battles of the Empire. He is young /and, moreover, this gentleman is a man of means. The wife of the hon. minister is well to do-it is far more cheerful, when you set out for the trenches, to leave your wife with enough to eat, as would say my good friend from Montcalm (M. Lafortune), to have some savings, and with her husband in the trenches, she will be comfortable during his absence.
Mr. Speaker, this conscription business will certainly lead to putting the two races

at loggerheads in this country. By the Confederation compact-the fiftieth anniversary of whioh we have just celebrated -it had been decided that both nations, English and French, would retain their rights and respect their obligations. What is more sacred to us, French Canadians, than our language, our faith, our religion; and the enjoyment of these privileges in the way that Englishmen in this country have it, is denied us in several provinces of the Confederation, is denied us by the majority of the people?
We are asked, we French Canadians, to go .and fight in France, in Flanders, to compel the Boches overseas, as they are called, or the Huns, respect the rights of the small nations; to have them respect Belgium's neutrality. That is very fine. But if, on the one hand, we, the French Canadians, are bound to go and see that the treaties, the agreements made by the great powers, be respected, to see that the rights of the weak be respected; I contend that, surely, in this country, the Englishmen should say: You, French Canadians of Quebec, you, French Canadians of Ontario and of Manitoba, you are weak, we shall give you your rights, and now enlist. There would be good sense in that. But, no, they maltreat the French Canadians, and then say: Enlist, go and defend those who .are being outraged across the ocean, but as for you, here, we'll keep on maltreating you, and go on just the same.
Mr. Speaker, I have stated it on many occasions in this House, and I do state it again that, as a French Canadian, and being myself of military age, I shall not vote, for anything in the fworld, in favour of a measure which might enlist me under such circumstances; I would not enlist. I have always declared, and I declare it again, that not one single Canadian should enlist when we see how we are at present treated in this country, for, Mr. Speaker, it is not only in Germany that Boches are to be found; there are some in Ontario and in Manitoba, they are to be found in both political parties. It is here, that we, the French Canadians, must stand up and tell them: which foe have we got to face. But why always persecute the French Canadian and tell him he is not doing his duty, when that majority in the country is forever interfering with our rights and will not even grant the French Canadians, in. this capital city of Ottawa, the right to have their children learn their mother tongue?
Is it a wonder now, if you go down into the province of Quebec, that among these same people, who know what is going on here, in Ontario, and in Manitoba, recruiting should be at a standstill? Mr. Speaker,
I say they are right, they should remain at home and await developments.
Now, as to this conscription Bill, whom will it cause to go and fight for the Empire and for France? It will reach only our poor people, while the folk of the Board of Trade of Montreal, of Toronto and of the whole country, that is to say, the big wigs, the millionaires, those who are coining money out of the war,^-as I see some of them in front of me, in this House,-these people have long been wanting conscription. They are in favour of conscription, they want the war to last as long as possible in order to hoard up still more millions.
We have even in this Government millionaires who favour conscription. Somebody has Spoken of conscripting riches- the conscription of wealth. I would be in favour of extending conscription to all the millionaires who want conscription. I want to be fair. I would exempt all those who do not speak of it, but for all the millionaires in favour of conscription, I would introduce another Bill in Parliament, I would bring in and submit a Bill which would not be No. 75, but No. 76, and I would say: all millionaires of the country in favour of conscription will be left with $100,000 the day after to-morrow, *and they shall retain no more, they will be allowed to start business over again, as in the past; but in the meantime they -shall be left with $100,000 only. Rightly ot wrongly,
I understand there are about 300 of these gentlemen in the country. It may be exaggerated, I do not know. If there be 300, according to what I mean to do, by seizing 90 per 100, that would make a fine amount. There are some having more than one million, some have five millions, ten millions. With such a sum of money, we -could send off 100,000 men, to suit these gentlemen. but I would want the men sent away on these .gentlemen's behalf, to be paid $3 .a day. That is not all. The wives of those soldier-s should be maintained, -during their husbands' absence, en the same style as the wives and children of these millionaires; that is to say, there would be no more use for this conscription Bill, land all these millionaires would be happy, since they want to continue the war and favour conscription. I think -that is the .best means to give them satisfaction.
Now, I have got several observations to' make. As I see on the other side, members who understand me, the hen. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) for instance, I beg

of him to transmit to the Prime Minister and to his colleagues, the message I suggest, as to the Bill I -would like to introduce.
Mr. Speaker, I spoke a moment ago of our millionaires of this country, of those very people who positively want to have 100,000 more Canadians sent over to the battlefields of Europe, in order to allow these gentlemen to make money. It is for this same reason that I suggest to the Government, when this conscription. Bill will have been disposed of by this House, that they introduce another Bill bearing No. 76, and the object of which would be to seize 90 per cent of these gentlemen's money, in order to send off these 100,000 soldiers and to pay them well. If my suggestion be not accepted by the Government, is it necessary to .send overseas 100,000 soldiers chosen among the people of this country, and that the Canadians remaining in the country provide for their expenses?
Let us first examine the present situation in Europe. England, so state .several members who have taken part in this debate, has, at the very least, three million men who are not enlisted, three million men who have not answered their country's call and whom compulsory service, such as it exists in England, cannot, reach. If my information is correct, there are at present in England, more than two million men ready to go and fight in France. I am further told that there are over a million young men, employed in the banks, in brokers' offices, in the theatres and in the moving-picture halls, who, like the others, are not yet enlisted. If .such is the case, Mr. Speaker, why should Canada be called upon to do more in this war than England? If it be true that this war is Canada's war, it is still a hundred times more true that it is England's war, because for our mother country it is a question of life or death. In this war England has at' stake the supremacy of the sea, and the supremacy of trade, whilst for us, for Canada, it would be no more, no less, only a change of master.
I do not mean to say, Mr. Speaker, that I would be ready to change masters, hut my idea is this one, that the outcome of the war is of much greater consequence for England than for us, because England is not used to be under master's lash, while, as far as we are concerned, we already have had two in the past and it would not be .so hard on us to have a third one. I have stated more than once, in my previous remarks, that we had no trenches to defend, and that is certainly true. The Government tell us that we should fill the gaps made in our

ranks by the foe and make good the terrible
losses sustained lately my the Allies. Have we not, in England, as I have just said, two million men that might serve for the same purpose? I will go further. For some time past we have a new ally in this conflict. The United States have just entered into the fray; if that country, with its population of 112,000,000 and the wealth of the whole world, if .that country, do I say, makes an effort, in proportion to the one made by Canada since the beginning of the war, that means that they should send into the trenches of France and of Belgium, from 6,000,000 to 7,000,000 soldiers. It seems to me that the United States are more interested than we are in this war; they have been attacked while we have not, their ships have been attacked and sunk with many lives on board. I, therefore, say to the Government: Do put a stop right off to this war craze and do not lead the people of this country at such a pace to ruin, when others, more interested than we are, having both people and wealth, can, without any apparent effort, furnish those 100,000 soldiers we were to send, and even more. That seems to me as logical as indisputable. There is not a single sensible man, knowing this state of things, that could reply, plausibly, I will say more, with a speck of common sense, that Canada has not done her duty. The whole country acknowledges that the effort made by Canada, i. e. the enlisting of more than 400,000 men, out of a population such as our own, deducting all the foreign races living on our territory, and also the numerous exemptions specified, is most worthy of admiration. I therefore maintain that Canada has contributed to the same extent as any other nation fighting under the Allied standards.
Now, were there any reason to impose conscription in this country, it seems to me that should rather have been done some eight or ten months ago, when Russia's efforts had somewhat slackened, being short both of arms and ammunition; the revolution which broke out in that country might have been considered a reason for the British colonies to make a greater effort. But, when all those clouds have rolled by, when Russia has recently fought such battles with as great a success as at the beginning of the war, when the entrance of the United States into the conflict puts at the Allies' disposal inexhaustible treasures of men and of money, I do not actually see why the Canadian people should be asked to further bleed themselves.

Both the United States and Canada have had quite recently the visit of an eminent British statesman, I mean the hon. Mr. Balfour, who was honoured in .the most important cities of the neighbouring republic, where he delivered quite a number of speeches. On every occasion, he always declared that the most urgent need of the present hour was not men, but ships, ships, and still more ships, as well as foodstuffs, for Europe was threatened with famine. He also came to Canada and did speak to the two Houses gathered in this hall. In his speech here, I do not find that he asked for soldiers, but on the contrary, he made a pressing appeal to the farmers, asking them to increase production for, did he say, foodstuffs are the great need of the present times He is not the only one, Mr. Speaker; other representative men,, no less eminent, have expressed similar views. In June 1916, Sir George Paish wrote in the Statist:
Victory over militarism will depend as much upon the farmers of the world generally and upon those of America and Canada, in particular, as upon the armies at the front.
In a recent number of the Echo de Paris, a noted writer, Mr. Maurice Barres, writes as follows:
We, the Allies, have the superiority of numbers and, in the Franco-British lines, we have even a million men more than the Germans facing us. As to the industrial supremacy, it is decidedly in our favour, on account of America entering in to the war. '
iln another French publication, ithe Paris Journal, Senator Humbert writes as follows :
Stocks are exhausted. The neutrals themselves have come down to the allowance system. The new arrivals are lessening in number. Famine is threatening the whole world. I had foreseen, some twenty months ago, the present consequence of this dreadful crisis, when I said : Let us spare our reserves. But I was not listened to, no more than when 1 demanded a year ahead guns and ammunitions. Is not the danger most apparent to-day? There is only one remedy: to call back from the front-lines two or three hundred thousand Frenchmen, of the older classes, and settle them once more on the land. Such are the necessary means of recuperation. The condition of the armies, the immense numerical superiority of the Allies, on the Western front, compared with their opponents, permit of adopting without delay this method of recuperation. Let us hurry, for it is already very late, and to-morrow, perhaps, it will be too late.
In, the face of these .statesment,s by .such eminent citizens, both in France and in England, I would like to know why the Government .still persists in sending over soldiers and yet more soldiers, when France
herself admits that it would be appropriate to recall home two or three hundred thousand men who are presently fighting in the trenches, in order to apply them to farm labour. Is it not true, Mr. Speaker, that, in Canada, the farmers cannot get the necessary labour, because these same people prefer to .go and work in the munition shops where they earn $3, $5 and even $7 a day? We, farmers, cannot pay such excessive wages, specially in the province of Quebec, where farming pays less than in the western provinces, where wheat is particularly .grown, although there may be other grain, but on a smaller scale. As forces, who aTe doing mixed farming, we cannot pay more than $30 per month for this kind of labour. I may frankly tell you that any farmer of the province of Quebec who would pay more than that, could not live there, .and .pay any interest however low the rate, if he owes anything on his land.
Now, you have also read in, the newspapers, the opinion of a man of this country, the largest manager, I believe, there i- in Canada, I want to speak of Baron Sbaugh-nessy, whose views evidently, are worthy of consideration. I am not .acquainted with him personally, I do not know his politics although I believe him to be a staunch Conservative, but, ,at all events, has he not, on more than one occasion, warned the Government? Has he not dome iit publicly, before the Montreal Board of Trade, in the presence of the ex-minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes) when he called upon him to stop volunteering? That was during the winter of 1916. Did he not warn us not to gi. too quick in the matter; .that the people of the country could not stand such an extravagance; that some day the bill would have to be footed, and that, if war was to keep on, said he, one year more, we, in Canada, would be at war a year and a half or two years after the others, because, as he .said, if you [DOT]really intend sending 400,000 men to the other side of the Atlantic, it will take at last a year and a half or two years before you get them back from the front. Therefore do I say, Mr. Speaker, that upon such .a statement, coming from .such an authority, from a man who knows out country so well; for he personally took a hand in its development .and he thoroughly knows our needs; knowing, .above all, what is going on across the seas, the *warning of this .man is most opportune. I believe that he came to Ottawa quite recently, he must have warned the Premier

i was not present-but, I really believe he must have warned him of the
