I will tell you what should happen after an election is held. Whoever the winner is-whether he be the right hon. gentleman who sits to your right, Mr. Speaker, or my revered and honoured leader-he should form a coalition Government to manage our state affairs until the war is over. If this can be done by the leader of the party that wins at the polte, a great service will be rendered to the people.
Each member of this House has the right -and a glorious heritage it is-to vote ae-

cording to his convictions. But, Sir, each member should do more than that. He should be vigilant in furthering the interests of his country, in season and out of season. Eternal vigilance is the price of liberty; it is the price that we must pay to maintain the privileges and the liberties that we have enjoyed in the past in this glorious young nation-a nation within a nation, the greatest Empire m the world.

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING AND ON THE AMENDMENTS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have felt some hesitation in dealing with such an important matter as that which is now submitted to the consideration of this House; but taking into account the present condition of pu jlic mind in this country, I think it my duty to show the reasons why I am opposed to the government measure ! I hope the House will pardon me if I have to go a few years back so as to show in stronger light the responsibilities incurred by the promoters of this Bill towards the electors of Canada. We are urged by the Government to insert in our statute book this proposal concerning a kind of military conscription which is called selective.
On the other hand, the Opposition want this measure to be beforehand submitted to the Canadian people and declares, through its authorized leader, that they will assist the Government in having it practically and immediately enforced should the majority of the people, consulted by way of a referendum, pronounce itself in favour of the measure, whereas my honourable friend from Berthier would have the House dispose of this bill forthwith by refusing, under the guise of the six months' hoist, to recognize its principle. The answer which I shall be ready to give when those several proposals are put to the House will be the direct outcome of my previous stand.
Having never complained of the fact that Canada was taking part in the present war, having, on the contrary, always approved of it in principle, I do not very well see how I could take upon myself to vote against the principle of conscription to-day, before the Canadian people are called upon to render their own verdict. Is it or is it not the wish of our people that its participation which, up (to this date, has been voluntary and free, should become obligatory and compulsory? It must be remembered that our Militia Act, drafted by Cartier and revised under Laurier in 1904, states clearly, in section 69, that, should volunteering not answer the purpose, the Government would have a right to resort to con. scription. In fine, do the Canadian peo-
190*
pie think that our soldiers, now fighting beyond Canada, are fighting for the defence of Canada? As far as I am concerned, I cannot deny the people the right to settle by themselves such a momentous and important question. I wish to know what they think of it, and I may add at once that, in accord with the leader of the Opposition, I shall abide by the judgment of the Canadian electorate. Accordingly, as I do not wish to substitute my own will to that of the people, clearly expressed by way of a referendum, and as I confess having no mandate, under the circumstances, to speak out what I think of the matter, I shall vote against the sub-amendment of the honourable member for Berthier. As for the amendment proposed by the honourable leader of the Opposition, it shall have my full support. And, in truth, I am unable to understand why the Government persist in denying the people, conscious as they are oi their power and aware of the baneful possibilities of its exercise, the right to decide such an important matter. At this critical hour of our national life the people would give this great question all thS attention which it deserves. Besides, be the conditions in a free country what they may, it is for the people to finally decide.
I am perfectly willing to admit that the Prime Minister is actuated by the best of intentions, by an intense patriotism, even; but I cannot admit, however, that he has the monopoly of that quality. Accordingly I think I should frankly state that, having neglected, from the outbreak of this war. to inspire his policy with the Canadian spirit, he would, no doubt, to-day be less fearful and apprehensive of a referendum " somewhere in England." Mr. Speaker, a question of capital importance for the welfare of Canada has been agitated for nearly ten years in this country, and it must be admitted that the proceeding in the course of this and former parliaments has been somewhat stormy ever since. In fact, during the session of 1910 a Naval Service Bill was introduced and adopted by Parliament in spite of the Opposition, then under the leadership of the present Prime Minister, who advocated the idea that the people should be consulted. Just think of it! We were to spend some ten million dollars to build in this country a navy which would be a Canadian navy and could assist the mother country in war time.
I have already said in this House and I repeat to-day that the Naval Service Act was the only cause for which the Laurier Government was driven from power, and as Cartier was defeated for having carried

through the Militia Act by means of which our defence on land was organized, so did Sir Wilfrid Baurier lose power because he had introduced and carried through his Naval Bill providing for our defence on sea. I owe it to history to say, however, that I took no part in the campaign against the Naval Act and its complements, a campaign which was carried on for nearly two years in the province of Quebec, under the paternal and benevolent eye of the present Prime Minister and of his Siamese brother the Minister of Justice. However, I did not suspect, at the time, that this doubledealing had no other immediate purpose than the triumph of the Tory party of old, over the policy of Baldwin-Lafontaine, MacNab-Morin and Macdonald-Cartier. True to the political principles of those men which alone had got me elected to this House, I did not hesitate, on two different occasions, to ask, by way of a resolution, full and complete justice for the Catholic or Protestant minority in the territory of Keewatin which was purported to be annexed to the province of Manitoba. Then again, at the following session, when the present Prime Minister, back from England, expressed, in the speech from the Throne, his desire to change the nature of our constitutional relations with the mother country, I did not hesitate for a moment to urge, also by way of a resolution, that our political and constitutional status should not be changed. That amendment was opposed by the Prime Minister, who stated that be could not accept it, because its adoption, said he, would preclude Canada from raising a finger for the defence of the Empire. During that same session I supported the leader of the Opposition in an effort to defeat the Government measure by which we were called upon to vote $35,000,000 as a contribution towards increasing the naval forces of the Empire.
Once more, on that occasion, I stated the grounds of my stand on that question, and honour be to the Canadian Senate who refused, in that case, to concur in the decision of the majority of this House! But, how fanciful the course of events, and how inconsistent the Tory policy! Those zealous apostles of the rights of the people as against the Laurier Naval Act, were then seen to refuse a plebiscite, or a referendum, and, God help me! general elections on this proposal of later date.
In the early days of this Parliament, Mr. Speaker, always for the sole purpose of remaining true to my promises towards the electors of my constituency, I hastened to ask the Government as to whether they in-

tended to make good the word given to the electorate of the whole country to the effect that the Naval Bill would be repealed as soon as they took office, and on the 4th of March, 1912, I asked the Government the following question:
1.	Is it the intention of the Government to propose that the Naval Act he repealed?
2.	If so, does the Government intend, should such repeal take place, to introduce another Bill expressing the views of the Government in this connection?
3.	If such further proposal is introduced, is it the intention of the Government to submit it to the approval of the people before it is
enforced?
To this question the Government answered through the Minister of Marine (Hon. Mr. Hazen) as follows:
The'answer to each of those three questions is : " Yes ".
I paid no heed to the diplomatic note which the honourable Minister of Marine thought it proper to append to the main part of that answer.
It is now np to the House and to the country to pass judgment as they see fit to do, in the light of the present events, .upon a Government so regardless of the most solemn pledges. As for me, I had the .satisfaction of having discharged my duty and, I was about to forget it, I had the .approbation of a man who, at the time, was a prospective senator of our province.
After all, I was easily comforted, from the 1st of August, 1914, the date on which the present war was declared, by the thought that the present Government which, up to that time, had, been unwilling to do anything towards organizing the defence of our country on sea, might at least, thanks to the foresight and, political genius of a statesman of our race, and I venture to say the greatest we have had since the days of Cartier, utilize our naval units for the protection of our coasts and provide for our most elementary defence.
Honourable members will perhaps understand a little more clearly that this statement of mine is neither gratuitous nor dictated by circumstances, when they have been made aware of the fact that, speaking at Shei'brooke, the queen city of the Eastern Townships in our province, previous to the present war, that is, on the 14th of May, 1913, I stated that, from the day England was engaged in a war threatening to the destinies of the British Empire, it would be the duty of Canada to assist the mother country. Who will say that the destinies of the British Empire are not at stake in the present war? Who will venture to claim

that, in the present war, England is not fighting for the most rightful and the noblest of causes? Let others give themselves up to minute and perhaps untimely inquiries as to the faults and errors of England; ias for me, I have no wish to scrutinize the hidden thoughts of the British statesmen and, in accord with Cardinal Merrier, I take the undoubted fact, the fact which nobody can deny: While Germany was violating clause 7 of the treaty signed at London on the 17th of April, 1839, by King Leopold in the name of Belgium, of the first part, and by the Emperor of Austria, the King of France, the Queen Of England, the King of Prussia and the Emperor of Russia, of the second part, England remained true to her oath. This I do not seek to minimize, but would rather seek to magnify, for it becomes a well-born child to commend all commendable acts of his forerunners. Therefore, faking into account the various events which have preceded and brought about the war, I have been and I am still of opinion that Canada should participate in this war voluntarily and freely. However, and I state it emphatically, I do not agree with those who believe that when England is at war, Canada is also at war. Proceeding from a normal and generous sentiment, this participation is one of a special character which if is most difficult to limit, and that is why I wish, first of all, that the Canadian people who, I think, are actuated by those same sentiments, should, of their own motion, determine that limit. It wouid not be so if the question were to fulfil and to execute 'an obligation; for, as a limit is necessarily implied in all obligations, that limit would be fixed and determined.
Mr. Speaker, I am not unaware of the fact that the present participation of Canada is helping France, and I am proud to be of French descent; but as England is fighting for England, so is my participation looking to Canada first and then to England the free institutions of which have so far preserved our nationality. That is why, in August, 1914-and I say this purposely-the Parliament of Canada was perfectly unanimous in voting, as a matter of urgency, $50,000,000 to pay the expenses of sending volunteers only. Need I quote, here, the words uttered within the precincts ,of this Parliament, on the 28th of May last, by A. J. Balfour, the great British statesman and democrat, who appreciated the nature of this participation in the light of the constitution by which we are governed?
The Government of the Mother Country cannot raise a corporal's guard in Canada,
Australia, New Zealand, or wherever you will; she can not raise a shilling of taxation; she has no power. (Hansard, House of Commons, May 28th, 1917.)
Unfortunately for Canada, its Militia Department was administered, at the time, by a man whose fitness for filling such an important position, even under ordinary circumstances might have been doubted. Redent developments made his position more important than that of the Prime Minister and it seemed only natural that the management of this department should be confided to some other than the regular representative of the Orange lodges. Nevertheless, and I have no hesitation in stating the fact, in spite of all outside as well as inside clamours, the Prime Minister continued his confidence in the Minister of Militia until the revelations of a commission which was extra-judicial and non-parliamentary-for more would have been known-forced the Prime Minister decidedly to break With the representative of the lodges who had made our military organization sectarian in its character to the extent that not only the French Canadians, but even the Anglo Canadians whose fitness was not recognized by a whole hive of middlemen, wearing, or not, the military uniform, were denied finding favour with the department.
Notwithstanding such difficulties, I may say it to the glory of our people, the system of voluntary enlistment succeeded beyond our most optimistic expectations.
Our military organization, under the direction of the Minister of Militia, was absolutely defective from the outset because it had the defence of the Empire rather than of Canada as its object. In a word, it was sought to have Canada play a leading part in this war, whereas, taking our financial position, our population and our resources into account, our help to England should have been limited to the exact proportion in which Canada could contribute. The Department of Militia was left for three years under the almost exclusive control of the member for Victoria and Haliburton as we may call him so now that he is sitting here with ns instead of taking his place in the trenches "somewhere in France," as he gave us to understand that he would do when he delivered a certain speech in New York, in which he first promised-before the Prime Minister did-ito send 300,000 soldiers from Canada, and even 500,000 if need be.
Untiring worker, since he left the cabinet he first thought of getting chosen

again as a Tory candidate in Victoria, where he met another opportunity to -abuse the French Canadians of this country at a political meeting held recently. A few days after, he came to the House and, in the absence of the Prime Minister, he put on the Orders of the' Day a resolution which entailed compulsory service for others.
Are we to presume that, when the Prime Minister was back here, he again yielded to the influence of this evil spirit? At any rate, in the same way that he had supported the request for 500,000 men, so did he introduce, just after his return from England, such a military conscription Bill as the ex-Minister of Militia said he desired.
History must have a very severe judgment in reserve for the men who, to-day, would turn this voluntary, free and generous contribution of our people into an obligation, and who, by the very fact, are paralysing the efforts of Canada while the! war is raging, the most portentous war England ever had to wage. In fact, and it should not be forgotten, Mr. Speaker, the untimely and, to express the whole of my thought, the unskilful manner in which the Prime Minister submitted this Bill to Parliament has alienated from him certain sympathies which he would now try in vain to get back. I would say, further, that the mature of the debate which has been carried on in this House for a fortnight, has caused every earnest listener to understand that one should rather take interest in the unity of Canada, henceforth, before looking to the unity of the Empire.
Certain English papers of this country, like certain 'members of this House, vie with each other in denouncing the disloyalty of the French Canadians who. they say, deliberately refuse to enlist and seem to have become unworthy of the consideration granted to all British subjects. Shall I say It? This movement against the province of *Quebec seems to be more especially mark-*ed in the province of Ontario, which would appear to have nothing more at heart than lio *ee Quebec isolated from the rest of Confederation. Unless I am mistaken about the intention of that province with respect to us, it is not at all unlikely that the conditions might be reversed and that the province which longed to isolate another should be isolated itself.
The Canadians of French descent have done their share in this war, if we consider the impediments of every kind and description which were set in their way. I shall only speak of the nature of those impediments in general terms, as several members

have dealt with it more in greater detail. Our people are attached to the soil upon which their ancestors have settled, and in their estimation, Canada is the only country worth while to them. When this country was conquered, the French Canadians were disarmed lest they should not willingly submit ito the new regime, and yet, the history of the struggles rendered necessary for the defence of our soil has recorded the names of no worthier defenders than they were. Not so long ago our gallant 65th Regiment did great honour to itself in the western prairies by calming an agitation by which peace and order were threatened in the interior of the country. By the way, may I recall, right here, the order according to which severe instructions were given a few years ago to the effect that this French regiment should present arms no more in honour of the Most High. What a sound military teaching, and what better means than this could be resorted to in order to make the sovereign power of the King of England more respected! The assertion is made repeatedly in certain quarters that the present Bill is aimed especially at the province of Quebec. I yet refuse to believe it. If it were so, now would be the time for us to investigate the real meaning of our political and constitutional status in this Confederation, the fiftieth anniversary of which we have just celebrated. We have attained manhood, and before we reach old age which would imply a heavier loss of the privileges guaranteed to us by Confederation, we shall seriously consider the advisability of asking that the federal covenant be set aside. There must he no superior race or inferior race in this country. Those who have associated together as a confederation must enjoy equal rights, and as to us, French Canadians, we have, so far, respected our obligations to the extent that the province of Quebec-and I do not hesitate to say it-may well be quoted as an example to all the rest of Canada for the fair treatment granted by her to minorities, within her limits, they enjoy all the privileges guaranteed to them by the constitution. Is it so, Mr. Speaker, with the minorities in the other provinces? Was it so - in New Brunswick in 1872? Has it been so in Manitoba ever since 1890? Is it so in this province of Ontario? Do our fellow countrymen enjoy a full 'and complete liberty in the matter of school teaching? As an answer to this, you hold out to us the letter of the law, but we appeal to the spirit of this same law, and adding hypocrisy to abuse, certain members of this House declare, at times, that rule 17 was adopted in

the province of Ontario, in order that the teaching of the French language in that province might be favoured to greater extent. No, long enough have statements of the kind been read by us with an excessive equanimity, and the House will allow me to recall, in this connection, the clatter indulged in by the lodges when the ex-Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) thought fit to have a postal card printed in English and French and distributed in Ontario as well as in Quebec. Ontario, have I said, is practically wrong in taking a position so inimical to minorities, because, in due time, all the minorities in Canada might perhaps adopt as their slogan that of the province of Quebec: "I remember". The province of Ontario has been all-powerful with the present Administration, she has made an ill use of that power, even, by the fact that she was instrumental in delaying, so , far, the construction of the Georgian Bay Canal, a national enterprise above all, and which would have brought about closer relations between the eastern and the western part of Canada, and the opening of the most direct route through the St. Lawrence river up to the head of the Great Lakes.
I should not conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker, without stating openly that I am not scared beyond measure by the furious outcry which may be directed against our
province

I say our province, for I am
confident that right-minded people of the great and beautiful province of Ontario are with us. We rely also on the farming community of the West to silence the ambitions, inordinate in many cases, of the Ontario manufacturers. As to our good friends of the Maritime Provinces, I do not think they would find any advantage in parting with their good neighbours of the province of Quebec. May the province of Ontario be inspired, at last, with a true Canadian spirit and never compel her sister provinces to .adopt measures for paralyzing her action so necessary to our national life, thereby averting the possibility of a central empire being created in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, it would have been my pleasure to address this House in the language of the majority, but as long as it will be sought in this province and outside of this House, to preclude the French children from learning the French languague at school, I shall deem it my duty to speak, here, the language guaranteed to us by the constitution, thanks to the efforts of the Liberal-Conservative parity, and in spite of the systematic opposition of the Tory party. So that no doubt is left in any mind as to the broadmindedness of the province of
Quebec in general and of the electors of the county which I have the honour to represent. I may say that the county of Ya-maska elected, for twelve consecutive years, as its representative at the local legislature the only English-speaking and Protestant elector who resided v/ithin the limits of that county, I mean the late Justice Wurtele.
Mr. Speaker, any one may call me a Conservative, a Nationalist or a Liberal if he likes; to my mind, a question of this nature admits of no party, we are guided solely by the sentiment which is in the heart of each of us.
However, I hope that after listening to me no one shall doubt that I intend henceforth to support the distinguished statesman who does credit to the Canadian Liberal party which under his far-seeing guidance represents, better than any other, heretofore, the true aspirations of our race.

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING AND ON THE AMENDMENTS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Loggie) has said that in this war we are fighting for Canada. That is quite true, but I think we should take a broader view of the struggle than that. There has been some discussion as to whether or not Canada is in any special danger on account of this war. Canada may not be in any special danger, but the world is in very grave danger. This is a world war, and will have world-wide effects, and the welfare of humanity is of more importance than even the welfare of Canada. We are citizens of the world as well as citizens of Canada, and I believe the real interest of humanity is to do our best in the winning of the war. I have been reluctantly forced to the conclusion that, in order to do our proper paTt, it is advisable that we should adopt the principle of conscription. I would he ashamed to admit that I had otherwise than reluctantly *come to a conclusion that would cause me to give a vote to force men to fight and, if needs be, to die in this terrible war. But having come to that conclusion I do not feel it is necessary for me to offer any apologies for differing from my leader on this question. I heartily concur in al'l that has been said in praise of the leader of the Liberal party by those who have felt it necessary on this occasion to differ from him. I have more confidence in the judgment of the leader of the Liberal party than in that of any other member of this House; but our actions must be guided by our own judgment and not by the judgment of someone else, and in voting on this question, I will follow the dictates of my conscience.

We on this side have received a great deal of advice from the press of this country on both sides of politics. We have been solemnly warned that we should not play politics with conscription, and we have been warned with equal solemnity of the result to our party if we should vote for a referendum; that is, we must not play politics on the question of conscription, but we must play politics on the. question of a referendum. I refuse to play politics on either question. The Journal-Press of this city on the 21st of June made the statement that I justified my willingness
To make bed-fellows of anti-conscriptionists on the ground that the grain growers' platform which I had signed, had contained the plank favouring a referendum.
I have never on any occasion, either to myself or to any one else, justified my proposed vote on any such ground. I know but one way to justify my vote on this question, and that is by voting as I believe to be right. The Journal-Press continues :
Even this hon. member would rush to the support of the Government if he thought there was any danger of the amendment carrying and the Government being defeated.
I do not purpose swallowing my convictions to save the Liberal party, .and I iam not going to swallow them to save the Conservative party. That is not the way in which parties are saved. I believe the Liberal party As well worth saving, but I do not believe the Conservative party is.
We have heard a great deal about the responsibility of the Government for the condition of affairs as it now exists and for the failure of recruiting. I quite agree that the Government is very largely responsible for .that condition, hut I think that the French Canadian agitators of Quebec and the anti-French agitators of Ontario must share the responsibility. I believe every hon. member of this House feels, from the bottom of his heart, that it is true that the control of the war organization of this country has been rotten with partisanship and patronage, and that is doing a great deal to upset the confidence of the people in the administration of affairs. The sooner that condition is remedied, the better.
I agree also that the failure to conscript wealth has had a great deal to do with the failure of the public to have in the Administration that confidence that is necessary in all cases. Let me quote, with approval now, a few words from the Journal-Press

of 26th of June on the question of the conscription of wealth:
* Knowledge on the part of all, that everybody was being made to do the utmost would be an addition of immeasurable strength to our effort.
Nothing can be truer than that statement. It is necessary at all times that there should be public confidence in the actions of the Government, and in the history of Canada there has been no time when that has been more necessary than the present, although it seems to me that our hon. friends opposite have failed to recognize the fact. We are ijold that we are raising as much from the wealth of the country as is needed to be raised from the wealthy classes for the purposes of the war. I do not believe that; I take issue with that statement immediately. We should have paid very much more than we have done of the war expenditures of the year from direct taxation which should be imposed upon the wealthy men of the country, and we should take less from the poor man through our outrageously high customs tariff. Further than that, we require to raise much more money each year to deal honestly with onr men at the front. We are paying them $1.10 a day, whereas unskilled labourers receive much more than that for perfectly safe work. A farm labourer in my locality can earn from $500 to $600 a year; he must get in addition three squares meals a day, regularly served, and he must have comfortable accommodation and bed or he will not stay. Our men at the front are in daily danger of mutilation and death; they are living in every discomfort that one can imagine; they are living in the midst of mud and dirt and surrounded by rats and vermin; they have to undergo all the horrors of war, and still we are not paying them as much as we pay our unskilled labourers. Some of the fiercest denunciations of the prophets of old were hurled against those who defrauded the labourer of his hire, but every day we are defrauding our labourers at the front of their hire, and now we are proposing to compel men to fight, and yet we are not going to pay them a reasonable wage for the suffering they will have to undergo. The fact that the Allies are not paying a reasonable wage is no excuse for us.
We hear a great deal about our duty to our boys in the trenches. The man who speaks most eloquently about our duty to our boys in the trenches is the man over military age, with a good income, who has no sons of military age, either in the trenches or elsewhere, who pays such sums

to the Patriotic and Eed Cross funds as do not inconvenience him in the least, and who pays his employees in comfort at home from $2 to $7 a day. Those whose hearts are in the trenches, whose flesh and blood are in the trenches, and in the hospitals and graves of France, cannot speak so glibly about these things. It is time we cut out this sentimental slobbering about our duty to our boys in the trenches until we are prepared to deal honestly with them.
We have heard a good deal about the probable working out of this measure, and I quite agree with the -hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) in his suggestions as to what the probable working out will be unless the provisions are materially changed. I do not purpose dealing with those provisions now. We shall have an opportunity of dealing with them later on, but they certainly must be drastically changed before this measure will be in anything like workable -shape. It may be that the Government, in bringing this Bill before us, is merely playing a political game. I' do not know whether that is the case or not, but we are placed in a certain position, -and I -am not going to discuss the question as to who is to blame for that position. We are placed in it and we must face it. It does not matter to me whether the Government is dealing with this question honestly or not; I must deal with it honestly, -and I purpose voting for conscription, because I believe it is the proper way in which to face the position in which we are placed. We have entered into the war for the benefit of humanity, and the obligation is on us to do our best to win the war as speedily as possible. That obligation is just as great upon us as it is upon Great Britain and France, and those countries have found it necessary to -adopt conscription, and it is advisable that we should do the same. The call for men, food and munitions is so great that it is necessary to get them with as little economic disturbance as possible, and it is only by selective conscription that that can be done. I have watched the work of recruiting in my own locality. In my own town a friend of mine is in charge of recruiting. Not a political friend but a personal friend. Were he a political friend he would not be in charge. My political friends may go to the trenches but that is the only possible connection with this war that is open to them, and that i's true of hon. members on this side generally. I believe that this friend of mine of whom I speak has done his work faithfully and well to the best of his -ability. He
has been well supported, but the work of late has been most unsuccessful.
The results are practically nil. It seems to me that the voluntary plan is wasteful at the present stage, and has been wasteful for the past eighteen months; it should have been changed at that time. Though I have Come to this conclusion I do not propose to criticise those who think differently. Each has to think this matter out for himself, and vote as he believes to be right. I believe that conscription was more needed a year ago than it is now, and that it would have been much more effective if it had been put in force then, but I would not have voted for it a year ago as I was not in favour of it then.
The Government, if they are honest, were opposed to conscription a few weeks ago. The Government are turncoats on this question, and so am I, but I do not propose to criticise those who do not turn their coats at the same moment as myself; I think it would be very bad taste.
We are asked to avoid playing politics on the conscription issue, but at the same time they ask us to be guided by the possible effects on our party of a vote for the referendum. If that is not playing politics, I do not know what playing politics means.
I do not approve of the way this conscription measure was brought before the House. I think it was as badly timed and as badly staged as it possibly could be. Neither do I approve of the way the referendum proposal came before the House. But conscription and the referendum are before us, and I propose to vote on the principle of conscription and on the principle of the referendum, no matter how they were brought before the House. If the Government will pledge themselves to submit the question of conscription to the people by way of referendum, if they desire the principle of the Bill to be first approved, I will support them. My own idea is that the best way should be to approve of the principle of the Bill, and afterwards get it in shape either before or after a referendum. The Bill could even be got in shape while the -people were getting ready to vote on the question. I will support the Government in whatever step they take so long as the question is first submitted to -the people. I propose to vote for submitting it to the people whenever I get the chance.
It has been argued that if it is right to take a vote of the people on conscription,

a vote should have been taken before we entered the war. I do not want to accuse any one of insincerity, but I can hardly see how any one who advances that argument can think for one moment that there is anything in it. It would have been absolutely impossible to have taken a vote on the question of entering the war; there would have been no time for it. More than that, in August, 1914, the public were practically unanimous that we should enter the war. It would have been utter nonsense to have taken a vote of the people on that question.
Two very large and very important sections of the community are now strongly opposed, not to carrying on the war, but to a certain plan for carrying on the war; they are strongly opposed to conscription.
I was in favour of direct legislation long before I became a member of this House. I placed myself publicly on record in favour of direct legislation before the principle was adopted as a plank of the platform of the Grain Growers' Association of my province. When the naval question was up in this House I suggested that the Government submit the question to the people in the form of a referendum. . Later on an amendment was moved .by a Nationalist member of the House that the measure be submitted to the people by way of referendum. I knew that a vote for the nationalist amendment would be unpopular with my leaders, but I believed it was right to vote for the amendment, and I voted for it accordingly.
It has been argued that we should not submit the conscription measure to the people by way of referendum because the measure would be defeated. Surely that is a horrible reason, with all respect to those who advance it. The fact remains, however, that for every man who gives that opinion publicly dozens give it privately. I believe the expectation that the measure would be defeated in a referendum is largely responsible for the opposition to the referendum amendment. What does that mean? We say that we are fighting in this war for democracy as opposed to autocracy. Now a democratic government, as I understand it, is government of the people, for the people, by the people, that is majority rule. What is autocracy? Autocracy is the rule of the many by a *select few, and some people want that select few to be hon. gentlemen in this House. They want the members of this House to rule whether the people approve or not; that is minority rule. I think those who urge us to vote against the referendum

because conscription would be defeated, are placing themselves in a peculiar position. They are asking our boys to fight and die for principles which they themselves refuse to put into practice. They would force our men to go out and kill Germans for fighting for principles which they themselves practise.
The Kaiser claims a divine right to rule Germany. Well, about a half a century ago the people of Germany selected an emperor to rule over them, and they provided means for the appointment of a successor to that emperor after his death. The German Emperor, on the strength of this, claims a divine right to rule. We were elected to this House some years ago. For what? To represent the people of Canada. But now some are claiming the right, not to represent the people of Canada, but to misrepresent them and to rule over them. What is the difference then, between the situation here and that in Germany? In Germany they have one big Kaiser, and in Canada we have a lot of little would-be Kaisers,-that is about the difference as I see it.
We are told that we must lead public opinion. But the proposition put forward
is,	not to lead public opinion but to muzzle
it.	I am quite willing to take my part in leading public opinion, but I do not care to take part in muzzling it. We are told that it would be better to have a general election instead of a referendum. No reason has been given for that, and I suppose that is because no reason can be given. Why should we adopt that plan unless for the purpose of finding out what the people want -getting the views of the people? But, if we want to get the views of the people, the simplest way is a referendum. After a referendum has been held we shall actually know what the people want. Why should we have an election? The only reason I can see is to confuse the issue and defeat the will of the people; I have not heard any other reason given. In a general election the issues will be obscured; and, so far as the boys at the front are concerned, very much obscured. If we ask the soldiers to vote for or against conscription, they will know what they were doing; but, with the present confusion of political parties in Canada, in a general election they would not know what they are doing; they might want to vote for conscription but at the same time they would be voting against it. I think that in most English-speaking constituencies the majority are in favour of conscription. But those in favour of conscription are divided into two parties. What would be the result? In the

constituency in which sixty per cent of the people are in favour of conscription and forty opposed to it, what are they going to do? The anti-conscriptionists are not fools altogether; there will be a Liberal conscriptionist nominated and a Conservative conscriptionist nominated. This will divide the conscriptionist vote, naturally anti-conscriptionists would win and that will mean minority rule. I do not know that that sort of minority rule would be very popular, or that it is just, fair and reasonable.
I am in favour of the referendum because I think it is the quickest way to get support for our men in the trenches. I am satisfied 'as to that, and cannot see an argument in support of any other plan. We could in a very few weeks havp the whole question settled by this means; and I am satisfied that if the question is fairly put before the people conscription will carry. I am willing to do my part in trying to have it carried. And I am prepared at all times to trust the people. While I try to make clear here what is the best plan, I recognize that, in this House, 'as in the country, the majority must rule. If the amendment in favour of a referendum is voted down, I will do what I can to make this Bill workable; 'and my feeling is that we ought all to do the same. But I say we should trust the people. I would like to make one last appeal to the Government to trust the people. If they do not trust the people how cam they expect the people to trust them? And why should the people trust them? If the Government refuse to .have faith in the people, I think that the people, at the firtt opportunity will hurl this faithless Government from power. But if we have faith in the people, we establish democracy in Government, which, we say, is the principle for which this whole war is fought.
Mr. LOUIS J. PAPINEAU (Beauharnois): (translation): Mr. Speaker, before proceeding with the remarks I have to make about the very important question now under consideration, I will take the liberty o/f calling attention to the statements made by some of the hon. members of this House.
The hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Cro-thers) has told ns that, if the province of Quebec had answered the call for volunteers as did the other provinces, there would have been no necessity for introducing a compulsory service Bill. The hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) assures us, on his part, that the province of Quebec will be the
least affected. The hon. member for North York (Mr. Armstrong) asserts as the raison d'etre of this measure that the French Canadian has not done his duty. The hon. Minister of Trade and Commei'ce (Sir George Foster) also deplores that efficient methods have not been adopted in Quebec, so as to educate the French population to the most important and vital questions raised by the present conflict. La Patrie of June 19, 1917, reproduced the following item from the Mail and Empire of Toronto:
The Mail and Empire admits that the Military Service Bill will affect Quebec more seriously than 'the other provinces.	.	.
When our volunteers offered themselves, did they make conditions? Did they say, "We will not go unless men from Quebec volunteer in due proportion?" They did not. And is French-speaking Canada, through the medium of recreant partisans of small calibre in English-speaking Canada, to dictate conditions in the matter of compulsory service?
There has not been equality of sacrifice. Quebec, with its large population, has not figured largely in the recruiting of the army. The Military Service Bill will rectify that inequality in so far as reinforcements are concerned. The 50,000 or 100,000 or whatever other number of new forces are to he raised to support our men at the front, will be drafted on a basis equitable to all the provinces. It is a measure to ensure equality of sacrifice.

The hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Arthurs) has told us 'there was not one available man in Ontario, and my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) states that in the city of Guelph, there are three or four hundred men he hopes to reach through this Bill.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, the object is compulsory service because, according to the quotations I have just read, the province of Quebec has shirked her duty. It is therefore, worth while to examine those various statements .and see whether they are well-founded or not. I will try to be brief and say very frankly what kind of .a situation has been made to that province, since the beginning of the war, as far as enlistment is concerned. I do not wish to repeat here what has already been said, but I will submit to you, Mr. Speaker, a few observations that may perhaps put the conditions in their true light.
Long before the month of August, 1914, the general impression was that a war, with the enormous armaments of the nations taking part in it, could not be of long duration. Europe, according to public opinion, expected the conflict ;and years had been spent in making the required preparations. The burden of armaments was crushing the n.a-

tions under ever increasing taxation and rendered, so to speak, the catastrophe inevitable. So, as soon as war had been declared, the general impression was that, with the modern war machinery, it might last only .a few months, six at the most. It has been lasting for almost three years and the end is not yet. However, in August, 1914, that impression of a most fierce and disastrous war, but of very short duration, did exist.
Enlistment and the levy of battalions in the province of Quebec were not conducted in such ;a way .as to encourage and induce the French Canadians to enlist. What were the intentions or the designs of those who organized recruiting? I believe that politics, here again, played a nefarious part.
I understand that, when the first contingent was organized, two French Canadian battalions were incorporated in it, and that five thousand French Canadians who tried to enlist, could find no place in those ranks. Later on, a French Canadian offered to raise a battalion, but his offer was turned down, English Canadians had been authorized to form other battalions and he should have to wait. Mr. so and so and Mr. another must be given the preference before a new authorization could be granted, which by the way, has never been given. There has been, as far as I can see, politics at the bottom of this whole matter. I cite this case, but is it the only one? Who can tell us there have not been many similar ones? I do assert that, even in this third year of the war, they still persisted in thwarting the recruiting among the French Canadians. I know that they may deny what I now say here, because I do not want to be formal- and I refuse to give any details. However, I believe that the facts I mention are well grounded.
In his speech, the hon. Minister of Mili- . tia (Sir A. E. Kemp) has mentioned the name of Lieut.-Col. A. M. Labelle. He told us that this officer had done all he could towards recruiting. My hon. friend from Saint Mary's (Mr. Martin) told him that Col. Labelle had three sons and that not one of them had gone to the front. I must say that, in fact, this officer has three sons, one aged 13, another 18, and the third, who is 22 years old, is in the service since August 7, 1914.
In 1914, there was in the Militia Department a patronage list, and on November 17, 1914, the name of Lieut.-Col. Labelle was placed on that list, as evidenced by the following letter:

Minister's Office,
Ottawa, November 17, 1914. Dear Colonel Labelle,
As requested by Mr. H. B. Ames, M.P., I have had much pleasure in placing your name upon the Patronage List of this department.
Faithfully,
(Signed) Sam. Hughes.
Lt.-Colonel A. M. Labelle,
34 Versailles St.,
.Montreal, Que.
What was the object of this proceeding?
I do not know. What I do know is that Lieut.- Col. Labelle was a good officer who had been 16 years in the Militia before the declaration of war. The Militia Council reports for the years 1912 and 1913 give praise to him and to his battalion. That of 1912 states that the commander of the [DOT] 65th Battalion is a zealous and enthusiastic officer, perfectly understanding his duties. In 1913, the Militia Council communicated to him the following remarks from the Inspecting officer:
A very line regiment and, thanks to the wonderful energy and zeal of its commander, it has made great progress at camp.
On September 9, 1915, Lieut.-Col. A. M. Labelle offered to recruit and organize a battalion for service in Europe and addressed his request to the ex-Minister of Militia. He stated that in the district where his battalion was being recruited, there were at least 400 men who would enlist under hi 5 command. Many had previously been in active service and all were trained soldiers. He wrote that he had been promised the funds required for the purchase of a machine gun, if he were permitted to raise that new battalion. He added that he had the co-operation of sixteen efficient officers and suggested as second commanding officer Capt. C. T. W. Etches, who had taken part in the South African War. As to his capacity for organizing and commanding this battalion, he referred the minister to his military record. . On October 14, 1915, he renewed his offer to the 4th Military District C. 0., dn Montreal. On October 25, 1915, he received an answer thanking him for his offer and informing him that, for the present, the organizing of a battalion for overseas service could not be considered.
Lieut.-Col. Labelle continued doing his duty and he did what he could, as the Minister of Militia declared before this House, in his speech of June 25. I believe they were wrong in refusing that offer.
Two months later, January 1, 1916, the Right Hon. Prime Minister raised his offer of soldiers for the overseas service to 500,000 men, and on July 16, 1916, the Minister of Militia made him a report wherein we read the following:

At the time you offered the half-million, it was as well known as it is now, that Quebec was not doing her duty, nor were some other parts of Canada doing theirs, although it must be borne in mind that the Acadians have done magnificently and I firmly believe that it is possible to get Quebec to fall into line later.
Recruiting was already ebbling and yet, two months previous, the formation of new battalions could not be entertained. In that same report, I read the following:
So far as recruiting for the future in Canada is concerned, your promise of half a million men could easily be fulfilled. But it will not be fulfilled, if you permit yourself to be hampered by raising little drafts here and little drafts there, sent over in charge of junior lieutenants.
If it was so easy as he said, I regret, and the whole country will regret it also, that he did not attend to it. I have just told you, Mr. Speaker, that in October, 1915, recruiting was not progressing. However, about that time, not later than January or February, 1916, a new battalion, the 206th was authorized. It was during the period when the Government authorized recruiting in localities where they could levy 25 men or more. That is what the ex-Minister of Militia mentions as the 3rd recruiting method, in his letter of July 5, 1916, which he quoted in the course of the debate. According to this system, I understand that the recruits were left in their own localities, it tney were 25 or over and could board there. They were paid $1.10 and 75 cents for their daily allowance. As these men were given to understand they would never leave the country, the proposition was an alluring one. And so the recruiting went on fine, but it did not last long, and in June, at Valcartier, a large number of these recruits unfit for service were discharged. One of them had swollen veins; another was flat-footed; another was ruptured; one or two w7ere maimed, having been the victims of some accident a few yers before their enlistment. I know that one of these had two fingers of his right hand missing. The battalion was disbanded, and a Montreal paper informed us that about ten of its officers were liable to pass before a military tribunal. I add, without further comment, that the commander of this battalion was an ex-Conservative candidate. There have also been other abuses and I wish to particularly refer to the enlistment of more youths of fifteen, sixteen and seventeen years of age, without their parents' consent and knowledge. Here are a few cases I may quote to the House: Israel Sauve,. enlisted in June 1915, at 16, in the
69th; Alfred Martin, No. 2158489, born May 23, 1901, enlisted March last in the 230th battalion of Ontario. It is a Forestry battalion, as I understand it. Armand Martin, born March 29, 1900, No. 1090400, and Ade-lard Faubert, No. 1090401, born January 26, 1900. All of them are French Canadians of the province of Quebec and are in battalions of the province of Ontario. I consider that these youths ought not to have been accepted, and that before long they will be returned home for the work is too much for them and they will probably be a burden to their families and to the State.
I mention these few facts in order to demonstrate how recruiting was carried on in a portion of the province of Quebec. Whence I infer that if volunteering has given only the results obtained and which are being so harshly criticized to-day-it is because the Government has not taken the proper means to obtain better ones, and did not care to do so. Complaints are being made, and rightly so, I believe, about the treatment given to the soldiers returned from the front, if I can judge by a case which I Tiappened to come across quite recently: Private Jos. Delisle was wounded at Ypres. He has his discharge, his conduct has been good. He received a bayonet wound in the right fore-arm, and a piece of shrapnel tore off his right elbow. He was laid- up for eleven months in various hospitals and convalescent wards. He returned to the country and was discharged at Quebec, on January 31, 1917. This soldier is twenty-six years of age and a married man. The Pension Commission, upon a report of advisers, which declare that his elbow-joint is anchylosed and that this incapacity is probably a permanent one, grant him a pension of $8 per month. He maintains that his elbow was torn off by a splinter of a shell, and I believe he ought to know what he's talking about. I do not intend to discuss this case, but I refer to lit in order to establish, with the other facts I have already related, that you cannot expect to get soldiers with such treatment. I do not want to take up the time of the House in repeating arguments against conscription, from the legal or the economic point of view, both of which have been so well and so thoroughly discussed. I will take the liberty of making only one remark upon this subject. Recently, I received ,a letter informing me that the Government intend calling in Chinese to take the places of the men they want to compel and send over to the front. My correspondent asserts that his representative, my hon. friend from Ohateauguay (Mr. Morris) has stated in

his own presence that the Govei'nment had already sent for 35,000 of them; that he had seen some of them at work and had been surprised to find them such good men. We are told that we need soldiers to fill the gaps, that we must go and relieve those who have gone away. We have promised to send them all the assistance in men that they might need, and for that, we must have conscription.
Who ever thought of conscription when these soldiers left? Who spoke of it? Nobody even thought of it. They went away as volunteers and they could not expect any but volunteers like themselves to join them at the front. If they ask for more than that, their demand is extravagant. And when the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) intimates that, if conscription is not adopted, the soldiers returning from the front may perhaps commit excesses to take revenge for not having received the desired reinforcements, if however they did desire any, I say that such language is an incentive to riot and to civil war without any plausible motive, and that he is uselessly trying to intimidate the country by such talk. The Right Hon. Prime Minister has on that occasion, spoken in terms unworthy of the high position he occupies.
I find it strange, but I am not surprised, when some honourable gentleman who boils with indignation at certain utterances of my honourable friend from St. Hyacinthe (Mr. Gauthier), finds fault with the speech of the Prime Minister which lends itself to some such interpretation.
We have in France and in England about 240,000 men, that is twelve divisions. There are four divisions, comprising 80,000 men, on the firing lines. If we deduct two more divisions for the auxiliary services, there still remain 6 divisions or 120,000 men on the reserve. It seems to me that in continuing the voluntary recruiting system, it would be an easy matter to supply the required number of soldiers, without resorting to conscription.
The New York Times of June 29 last, commenting on the fact that' the American troops will be commanded by their American general and independent of all other control-but this General consulting and acting in concert with the commanders of the French and British armies, says that this will prevent jealousy and discontent, as was the case for Canada, because our soldiers, under the orders of the British authorities, have suffered hardships.
Are our soldiers sent more often than in their turn to the most exposed points? One

might believe it. If such were the case, we must expect not only a levy of 50,0C0 or 100,000 men, but that many others will have to follow, and sooner than is generally expected.
After having announced his conscription policy, the Prime Minister proposed to the leader of the Opposition to form .a coalition ministry, in order to have this measure adopted, and afterwards call for a general election to have this Act approved by the electorate. The Right Hon. Prime Minister contends that the seriousness of the situation made his coalition proposal not only desirable but even necessary. The parleying came to nothing, the Right Hon. leader of the Opposition stating that he could not accept a coalition having conscription as a basis. These negotiations were continued from May 24 to June 6.
The debate upon the second reading of this conscription Bill was opened June 18. On the 19th, the ex-Minister of Militia made this assertion :
It is a well known fact that up to two weeks ago, distinguished members of the cabinet seated that there would be no compulsory service.
So, while negotiations were going on to have a coalition based upon conscription, having conscription as its essential condition, some ministers were declaring that there would be no compulsion. During these coalition negotiations, the Government entered on the Orders of the Day the Railway Act, which they had already introduced and then withdrawn in 1913. They might have even added the Naval Act, as a guarantee of their good faith. These two measures, being the most controversial of this Parliament, might well have been included in the henceforth famous coalition scheme.
Mr. Speaker, if conscription had been, I will not say necessary, but only useful to maintain Canada's effort in this war, it should have been easy for the Prime Minister to demonstrate that fact to the hon. leader of the Opposition. Had there been urgency, as it is said, it would have been so much easier to show it. Under such circumstances, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister had no need to offer a coalition government; in my opinion, it was an insult freely given, and a miserable political manoeuvre for purely political ends. No, there was no necessity for a coalition of the political parties. I very well know, and nobody doubts it, in this House and in the country, that if the conscription measure proposed by the Government had been nec-

essary, the Eight hon. leader of the Opposition would have so declared it, and while demanding that it be submitted to the people, he would have at the same time asked the people to approve it. The Opposition leader's patriotism is not based or dependent on either coalition or any political combination whatever. In truth, the idea of proposing the coalition of the political parties to pass a conscription Bill and then, by means of this union of both parties, resort to elections in order to enforce it on the people, is distinctly Tory. And, indeed, it did come and it could only come from a Conservative government. If the proposition to adopt this Act and then have an election to have it ratified is reasonable and for the general good of the country, and not merely a political manoeuvre, why do not the Government adopt that policy? They have only to consent to consult the people and the Bill will go through to-morrow.
In moving his amendment to the amendment, the hon. member for Berthier (Mr. Barrette) stated that he had received from the various parishes of his county resolutions or petitions from his constituents demanding the referendum or elections, and he inserted in Hansard the very text of one of these resolutions.
The Government having stated taeir intention to have this Act adopted without referendum or elections, it seems to me that, if the hon. member for Berthier wished to comply with his electors' demand, he had only to vote in favour of the referendum proposed by the Eight hon. leader of the Opposition, or else ask for general elections. But no, that did not suit the hon. member's purpose. His electors ask him a popular consultation, referendum or election, and he does not want them to decide the question themselves.
As this Parliament has no longer any legal existence and as we are here because we have voted ourselves an extension of time, it seems to me that the request of our electors, or rather of the electors of our counties-they are no longer electors, strictly speaking, since the month of October last-it is we who have appointed ourselves their representatives, it seems to me, therefore, that we should strictly comply with the requests they may submit to us, especially upon such an important question.
I have also received, Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for Berthier, resolutions from the electors of my county, demanding a popular consultation. They ask that the question now under consideration be submitted to their own decision. I consider this demand entirely legitimate and reasonable. I shall not assume to decide it for them and, consequently, I will vote against the amendment to the amendment, in favour of the amendment asking for a referendum, and against the adoption of this Bill, so long as it has not been submitted to the Canadian people for approval.

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING AND ON THE AMENDMENTS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my apology for addressing you at this late hour is that I do not desire to give a silent vote on this important question. When we look at the flags of the Allies with which this. Chamber is decorated, we are reminded that at the commencement of the war, if * the British Empire, to which we belong, had stood aside and remained neutral, permitting the German Empire to crush France, we and the Empire generally would have been spared a great loss of our manhood and a great outpouring of our wealth. But if the Empire had taken this course, would we, as Canadians, have been proud of our connection with the British Empire? No, Sir, I think that if the Empire had taken such a course, the feeling in this country would be in favour of tearing down the British flag and starting out as an honest independent and self-respecting nation. We as Canadians would never have endorsed such a course.
The .object of the Bill now before the Louse is to obtain further men for the b ittle-front. Marshal Joffre, when in Montreal, emphasized the need of Canada sending more men. Sir Arthur Currie, the present commander of our forces in France, sent out a call to Canada to come over and help relieve the over-worked battalions who have been subjected to a great strain for the past two years and longer.
The number of voluntary enlistments in Canada has been a source of great pride to us and has far exceeded our expectations; but, at the same time, there are quite a number who could be spared and who would go if a campaign to secure further enlistments were started by the members of this House, with the object of winning the war instead of trying to obtain party advantage. The mover of the amendment which calls for a referendum (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) said that Canada was not in danger *of being invaded, which strengthens my opinion that he is not heartily in sympathy with sending men to Europe. The hon. member for North 'Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) stated that he was against the Bill hut favoured

the amendment owing to the fact that he , wished to follow his leader. This reminds me of an incident at the battle of Killi-crankie. Scotland was invaded by a foe and the Government mustered the clans and appointed a leader. On the day of the battle two of the clans did not appear. Instead they hid behind crags and on the moors, and acted as the hon. gentleman is acting, simply because their chief, for certain reasons, refused, on the day of battle and trial, to join heartily with the rest of his country. We have here two regiments; some of the Liberals from the lower provinces and the province of Quebec are like snipers; they stand back when the country is invaded and refuse to take their part in its defence, simply and solely, according to their arguments, because of their great respect for their leader. The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) insinuated that the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Sevigny), was responsible for the poor recruiting in Quebec owing to alleged statements of six years ago, and he emphasized the fact that the minister was at that time thirty years old. We remember the time when the hon. member for St. John was forty years old and ran a campaign in St. John against his present leader, when he *would not support Sir Charles Tupper, the leader of the Conservative party, in the elections of 1896, nor would he support the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier)-he wanted to become the leader of a party of his own. I wish that at some time he would explain to this House his reasons for that course. He now appears to have a great admiration for. the right hon. gentleman. Judging from the speech of the hon. member for St. John, everything in connection with the war is being done wrong. You would imagine that the hon. member knew considerably more than General Haig or General Joffre, judging by the way he lectured the Government on their conduct of the war.
Much has been said about conscription of wealth and the imposition of an income tax. That is a serious problem that at an early date will have to be faced. Let me remind you that Canada to-day is practically on its own resources as to borrowing. We have large debts maturing, and these we shall be obliged to finance ourselves. Last year the revenue taken from the people was $230,000,000, almost $1,000,000 more than the usual amount. In addition to that, during the last two years there has been a very large contribution of money by the people of Canada i about $500,000,000 has been infMr. Nicholson.]
vested in war bonds by Canadians. I fear that before long there will be a stringency in the money market, so it is not wise to withdraw too much money from the people of Canada to-day. That is why it is not desirable at this time to devote too much money to the retirement of maturing debts.
When this war is over we will have increased taxes, and it will tax the ingenuity of the Finance Minister and Parliament to provide ways and means. I would suggest that an increase duty be placed on cigars, cigarettes and imported raw leaf cigar wrappers as high as 200 boxes, so as to encourage the growth of thait style of leaf in this country. Twenty years ago the United States placed a duty, of $1.85 on cigar wrappers. Now the best wrappers in the world are raised in Connecticut, owing to protection provided. The climate of some parts of Quebec is well adapted to raising that kind of leaf. In fact, it has been demonstrated. There is another suggestion made by Mr. W. F. Maclean, of York, and, if the facts are as he alleges with regard to nickel product, a large revenue could be obtained by imposing an export on thait commodity, which is indispensable for the manufacture of certain articles.
In conclusion, I would appeal to my friends from Quebec to hold another caucus and place their great leader in his proper place amongst the statesmen of the Empire, by withdrawing the amendment and supporting the Bill. Let us all go to our constituents as serious men facing a great emergency. If you do not do so you place your leader and yourself in a position of antagonism to the rest of Canada, yes, further, to the United States, leave England out if you will, but what of France? We have heard Viviani, .also Marshal Joffre, whose emphatic call w>as for men.
Mr. Speaker, I intend to vote for this Bill, because I remember the Lusitania incident, where that ship was torpedoed without warning, and men and women were heartlessly drowned. I remember, also, of the cruel murder of Edith Cavell, an .angel of mercy, who was taken and heartlessly executed by this cruel German power. I remember, also, our friend, who used to sit alongside of me, who is now in a grave in France. I refer to our late colleague, Mr. Harry Baker, who sacrificed his young life in the interests of his country. There is another voice, Sir, in connection with this question, and that comes from Germany. It is not the Kaiser nor Hindenburg, but the voice of a colleague in this House, who was taken from his young bride, and in-

eareerated in a German prison and held there three years. When his wife died, they would not let him view the remains, even if accompanied by a guard. Things like that make me feel that I should support this Bill, in order to send men overseas tp assist to break down the power of that nation, which is a menace to civilization. I am rather surprised at the tactics of the Opposition. It is well to have two political parties in this country, but I do not think the Liberals, especially those from Quebec, are treating their leader properly, and he is not treating the country as he should. He has been loyally supported in the lower provinces. At one time he had a solid eighteen supporters from Nova Scotia. Gentlemen rise in Parliament and blame his defeat on what? On Mr. Bourassa. They say he is the man who defeated them. I desire to say that I would not be in this House now, were it not for the issue that was placed before the country by the Liberal party in the election of 1911. The county I represent was in favour of the Liberal party, but that party was defeated solely on the reciprocity issue. The people of this country, not only in the lower provinces, but in Ontario and Quebec, largely turned against the Government on that question. It appears to me foolish for a gentleman to state that the people of this country are carried away by appeals to prejudice. I do not believe that anything ,of that sort will have any weight, and I do not think such appeals will place the country in a better position. What will be said when the vote is taken tomorrow night? Supposing one corner of Canada is against the remaining provinces, you are putting your leader up against the sentiment of the whole country. What will be said in London after the vote is taken? Surprise will be expressed. What will be said in France? Berlin, no doubt, and Vienna will be pleased. Constantinople, especially, will rejoice. You are backing up a power which has massacred the Armenians, and, by your conduct in voting against this measure, you are upholding the rule and power of Turkey.

Mr. Speaker, I beg to inform you that I am desirous of addressing the House after the learned member who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Nicholson, Queens, P.E.I.); but in view of the lateness of the hour it seems to me that it may be deemed a hardship to detain the House any longer.
Therefore, I move the adjournment of the debate.
